'''Te Pāti Māori''' ({{IPA|mi|tɛ ˈpaːti ˈmaːɔɾi}}) is a left-wing [[political party in New Zealand]] that advocates [[Māori people|Māori]] rights.<ref name=":6" /> Founded as the '''Māori Party''' in 2004, it changed its name to Te Pāti Māori in 2023. Except for a handful of [[New Zealand electorates#Electorates in the 53rd Parliament|general electorates]],<ref>{{Cite web |title= Kelston candidates |url= https://vote.nz/2023-general-election/about/2023-general-election/electorate-candidates/?ElectorateType=General+electorates&Electorate=Kelston&action_filter=View+candidates |access-date=29 September 2023 |website=Vote NZ |archive-date=29 September 2023 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20230929033357/https://vote.nz/2023-general-election/about/2023-general-election/electorate-candidates/?ElectorateType=General+electorates&Electorate=Kelston&action_filter=View+candidates |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Te Pāti Māori candidate tops informal audience poll at chamber event |url= https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2023/09/28/te-pati-maori-candidate-tops-informal-audience-poll-at-chamber-event/ |access-date=29 September 2023 |website=Te Ao Māori News |archive-date=29 September 2023 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20230929100125/https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2023/09/28/te-pati-maori-candidate-tops-informal-audience-poll-at-chamber-event/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Te Pāti Māori announces Merepeka Raukawa-Tait will fight general electorate seat |work=[[Newshub]] |url= https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2023/07/te-p-ti-m-ori-announces-merepeka-raukawa-tait-will-fight-general-electorate-seat.html |access-date=29 September 2023 |archive-date=15 October 2023 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20231015005458/https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2023/07/te-p-ti-m-ori-announces-merepeka-raukawa-tait-will-fight-general-electorate-seat.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> it contests the reserved [[Māori electorates]], in which its main rival is the [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour Party]].

Under the current parliamentary leadership of [[Rawiri Waititi]] and [[Debbie Ngarewa-Packer]], it has policies of upholding {{lang|mi|[[tikanga Māori]]}}, dismantling [[structural discrimination in New Zealand|systemic racism]], and strengthening the rights promised in {{lang|mi|[[Te Tiriti o Waitangi]]}},<ref>{{Cite web |title=Te Pāti Māori |url= https://www.maoriparty.org.nz/ |access-date=26 June 2022 |website=Te Pāti Māori |archive-date=16 August 2023 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20230816105403/https://www.maoriparty.org.nz/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=31 May 2022 |title=NZ Māori party rules out right-wing coalition after next election |url= https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/may/31/nz-maori-party-rules-out-right-wing-coalition-after-next-election |access-date=26 June 2022 |website=[[The Guardian]] |archive-date=4 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230604230944/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/may/31/nz-maori-party-rules-out-right-wing-coalition-after-next-election |url-status=live }}</ref> including {{lang|mi|[[tino rangatiratanga]]}}<ref>{{Cite web |date=6 August 2021 |title=Mana Motuhake |url=https://www.maoriparty.org.nz/mana_motuhake |access-date=26 June 2022 |website=Te Pāti Māori |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":4" /> (Māori sovereignty). It is also committed to a mixture of [[democratic socialism|socially progressive]] and [[green politics|green]] policies through a "{{lang|mi|Tiriti|nocat=y}}-centric" lens.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=31 May 2022 |title=NZ Māori party rules out right-wing coalition after next election |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/may/31/nz-maori-party-rules-out-right-wing-coalition-after-next-election |access-date=17 July 2022 |website=[[The Guardian]] |archive-date=4 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230604230944/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/may/31/nz-maori-party-rules-out-right-wing-coalition-after-next-election |url-status=live }}</ref> This includes removing [[Goods and Services Tax (New Zealand)|Goods and Services Tax]] from food, opposing [[Deepwater drilling|deep sea drilling]], organising and funding a [[Māori Health Authority|Māori health authority]], lifting the minimum wage to $25 an hour, returning [[Department of Conservation (New Zealand)|Department of Conservation]] land to Māori control ({{lang|mi|[[kaitiakitanga]]}}), and reducing homelessness.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |date=31 May 2022 |title=New Zealand's next kingmakers: who are the Māori party? |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/may/31/new-zealands-next-kingmakers-who-are-the-maori-party |access-date=26 June 2022 |website=[[The Guardian]] |archive-date=10 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230810230339/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/may/31/new-zealands-next-kingmakers-who-are-the-maori-party |url-status=live }}</ref> Since Waititi and Ngarewa-Packer became leaders in 2020, the party has been described as [[left-wing politics|left-wing]],<ref name=":5">{{Cite news |title=NZ Election 2020: John Tamihere picks unlikely preferred coalition partner for Māori Party |work=[[Newshub]] |url= https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2020/09/nz-election-2020-john-tamihere-picks-unlikely-preferred-coalition-partner-for-m-ori-party.html |access-date=27 January 2023 |archive-date=27 January 2023 |archive-url= |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="auto1">{{Cite web |last=Johnson |first=Glen |title=Ardern vs Collins: New Zealand is at a crossroads |url= https://web.archive.org/web/20230323092839/https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2020/10/11/new-zealand-elections-4/ |url-status=live }}</ref> and [[progressivism|progressive]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title='Incredible result': Māori Party returning to Parliament |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/election-results-2020-maori-party-back-in-parliament-as-rawiri-waititi-wins-waiariki/U2KUOHTTTYXCW3WMSN4U7IH25E/ |access-date=27 January 2023 |website=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |archive-date=2 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230802025206/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/election-results-2020-maori-party-back-in-parliament-as-rawiri-waititi-wins-waiariki/U2KUOHTTTYXCW3WMSN4U7IH25E/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":5" /><ref name="auto">{{Cite web |last=Godfery |first=Morgan |title=Is Labour hostage to its centrist base? |url=https://www.metromag.co.nz/society/is-labour-hostage-to-its-centrist-base |access-date=27 January 2023 |website=Metro |archive-date=8 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230208212200/https://www.metromag.co.nz/society/is-labour-hostage-to-its-centrist-base |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Tariana Turia]] founded the Māori Party after resigning from the governing Labour Party, in which she served as a [[ministers in the New Zealand Government|minister]], over the [[new Zealand foreshore and seabed controversy|foreshore and seabed ownership controversy]]. She and [[Pita Sharples]], a high-profile academic, were the first co-leaders. The party won four Māori seats in the [[2005 New Zealand general election|2005 election]] and went into Opposition. After the [[2008 New Zealand general election|2008]], [[2011 New Zealand general election|2011]] and [[2014 New Zealand general election|2014 elections]], where the party won five, three and two Māori seats respectively, it supported [[Fifth National Government of New Zealand|a government]] led by the centre-right [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]],<ref name="Marsh-Miller">{{cite book |last1=Marsh |first1=Ian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=i04gAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA284 |title=Democratic Decline and Democratic Renewal: Political Change in Britain, Australia and New Zealand |last2=Miller |first2=Raymond |date=2012 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-139-53701-8 |page=284}}</ref> with the Māori Party co-leaders serving as [[New Zealand Government#Ministers outside Cabinet|ministers outside cabinet]]. During this time, the party advocated more moderate politics.<ref name="auto2">{{Cite web |last=Godfery |first=Morgan |title=The rise and rise of Te Pāti Māori |url= https://www.metromag.co.nz/society/therise-and-rise-of-te-pati-maori |access-date=27 January 2023 |website=Metro |archive-date=27 January 2023 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20230127030856/https://www.metromag.co.nz/society/therise-and-rise-of-te-pati-maori |url-status=live }}</ref>

The party won no seats in the [[2017 New Zealand general election|2017 election]],<ref name="2017 general election results">{{cite web |title=2017 General Election – Official Result |url= http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/ |access-date=24 September 2017 |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]] |archive-date=7 October 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171007120051/http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/ |url-status=live }}</ref> which was attributed to backlash for their support of National.<ref name="auto2" /> Under new leadership they returned to parliament in the [[2020 New Zealand general election|2020 election]] when Waititi won the [[Waiariki (New Zealand electorate)|Waiariki]] electorate. Although the party's share of the country-wide [[party vote]] declined marginally from 1.18% in 2017 to 1.17% in 2020, winning Waiariki gave the party full proportional representation and two [[Member of parliament|members of parliament]], with co-leader Ngarewa-Packer becoming a [[list MP|list member]].<ref name="RNZ 6 Nov 2020" /> Waititi joined Ngarewa-Packer as co-leader in October 2020 and the pair led the party to win six electorate seats and 3.08% of the popular vote in the [[2023 New Zealand general election|2023 election]].<ref name="2023 results">{{cite web |date=3 November 2023 |title=2023 General Election – Official Result |url= https://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/index.html |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20231104213043/https://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/index.html |archive-date=4 November 2023 |access-date=17 November 2023 |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]]}}</ref> In 2025, the national council voted to expel MPs [[Mariameno Kapa-Kingi]] and [[Tākuta Ferris]] from the party. On 10 March 2026, a High Court ruling reinstated Kapa-Kingi.

== History ==

=== Formation ===

The origins of Te Pāti Māori can be traced back to the 2004 [[New Zealand foreshore and seabed controversy|foreshore and seabed controversy]], a debate about whether the [[Māori people|Māori]] have legitimate claim to ownership of part or all of New Zealand's [[foreshore]] and [[seabed]] that arose during the [[Fifth Labour Government of New Zealand|Fifth Labour Government]]. A court judgement stated that some Māori appeared to have the right to seek formal ownership of a specific portion of seabed in the [[Marlborough Sounds]]. This prospect alarmed many sectors of New Zealand society however, and the [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour Party]] foreshadowed legislation in favour of state ownership instead. This angered many Māori, including many of Labour's Māori MPs. Two MPs representing [[Māori electorates]], [[Tariana Turia]] and [[Nanaia Mahuta]], announced an intent to vote against the legislation.<ref name="Morgan Godfery pp. 240-241">Morgan Godfery, "Chapter 4.4: The Māori Party," pp. 240–241.</ref>

Turia, a junior minister, after being informed that voting against the government would appear "incompatible" with holding ministerial rank, announced on 30 April 2004 her intention to resign from the Labour Party. Her resignation took effect on 17 May, and she left parliament until she won a [[2004 Te Tai Hauauru by-election|by-election in her Te Tai Hauauru seat]] two months later. After leaving the Labour Party, Turia, later joined by Sharples, began organising a new political party. They and their supporters agreed that the new organisation would simply use the name of "the Māori Party". They chose a logo of black and red – traditional Māori colours – incorporating a traditional [[koru]] design. The party constitution provides that there are two party co-leaders, one male and one female.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=12 October 2019 |title=Māori Party Constitution |url=https://elections.nz/assets/Party-rules/maori-party-rules-and-constitution-2019.pdf |access-date=27 October 2020 |archive-date=30 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201030014500/https://elections.nz/assets/Party-rules/maori-party-rules-and-constitution-2019.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> Turia and Sharples were the first to fill these roles. They indicated that they wished to unite "all Māori" into a single political movement.<ref name="Morgan Godfery pp. 240-241" /> The party was formally established on 7 July 2004.<ref name=Ngatai2013>{{cite press release |last=Ngatai |first=George |title=George Ngatai – Standing for President of Maori Party – Speech |url=http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PO1307/S00187/george-ngatai-standing-for-president-of-maori-party-speech.htm |date=16 July 2013 |agency=Scoop |access-date=17 August 2019 |archive-date=10 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230810235551/https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PO1307/S00187/george-ngatai-standing-for-president-of-maori-party-speech.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== 2005 election and first term in Parliament ===

In the [[2005 New Zealand general election|2005 election]], the Māori Party won four out of seven Māori seats and 2.12% of the party vote. The latter entitled the party to only three list seats, so the fourth electorate seat caused an [[overhang seat]]. In the election night count, the party vote share was under 2% and the Māori Party would have got two overhang seats; when the overhang was reduced to one, National lost a list seat that they appeared to have won on election night. Tariana Turia held Te Tai Hauauru; [[Pita Sharples]] won the [[Tāmaki Makaurau (New Zealand electorate)|Tāmaki Makaurau electorate]]; [[Hone Harawira]], son of [[Titewhai Harawira]], won [[Te Tai Tokerau]]; and [[Te Ururoa Flavell]] won [[Waiariki (New Zealand electorate)|Waiariki]].<ref>Morgan Godfery, "Chapter 4.4: The Māori Party," pp. 243–244.</ref>

In the post-election period the Māori Party convened a series of [[hui (Māori assembly)|hui]] to decide whether to support Labour or National, though some party leaders indicated they preferred to deal with Labour. National Party deputy leader [[Gerry Brownlee]] and leader [[Don Brash]] tried to win over the Māori Party and claimed that it would support National to form a government, although Turia denied this.<ref>{{cite news |last=Young |first=Audrey |date=19 October 2005 |title=Brash: I had the 57 votes |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/event/story.cfm?c_id=1500891&ObjectID=10351002 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Crewdson |first=Patrick |date=16 October 2005 |title=Coalition talks in chaos as Nats accuse Clark of failure |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/section/story.cfm?c_id=1&ObjectID=10350478 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author=Tony Gee, Audrey Young and Ruth Berry |date=7 October 2005 |title=National courts the Maori Party |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/event/story.cfm?c_id=1500891&ObjectID=10349075 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |access-date=9 January 2006 |archive-date=30 September 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930014447/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/event/story.cfm?c_id=1500891&ObjectID=10349075 |url-status=live }}</ref> She met privately with prime minister [[Helen Clark]] and ruled out a formal coalition. Later, the Māori Party decided to remain in opposition and not be part of a Labour-led government.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/event/story.cfm?c_id=1500891&ObjectID=10350828 |title=Maori Party stays in opposition |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=18 October 2005 |access-date=9 January 2006 |archive-date=30 September 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930014311/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/event/story.cfm?c_id=1500891&ObjectID=10350828 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

On 24 January 2006 the Māori Party's four MPs were jointly welcomed to [[Rātana pā]] with Brash and a delegation of eight National MPs. They had been intended to be welcomed on half an hour apart but agreed to be welcomed and sit together. Turia disputed claims that this was pre-arranged, saying: "We're here for a birthday. We're not here for politics."<ref>{{cite news |title=Taking partners for Ratana waltz |first=Haydon |last=Dewes |work=[[The Dominion Post (Wellington)|The Dominion Post]] |date=25 January 2006}}</ref> However critics said this would have reminded onlookers of how the Māori Party and National were said to be in coalition or confidence and supply talks. This may also have served to reinforce the Labour Party's election campaign statement that a 'vote for the Māori Party is a vote for National'. One Rātana kaumatua (elder) said this was deliberate and deserved after the talks.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/category/story.cfm?c_id=280&ObjectID=10365240 |title=Parties forced to share stage at Ratana marae |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=25 January 2006 |first1=Jon |last1=Stokes |access-date=24 January 2006 |archive-date=29 September 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929173724/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/category/story.cfm?c_id=280&ObjectID=10365240 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Supporting a National-led government: 2008–2017 ===

In the [[2008 New Zealand general election|2008 general election]] the Māori Party retained all four of the seats it won in 2005, and won an additional seat, when [[Rahui Katene]] won [[Te Tai Tonga]] from Labour. Two seats were [[overhang seats]]. The party's share of the party vote rose slightly to 2.39%.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2008/partystatus.html |title=Official Count Results – Overall Status |access-date=23 November 2008 |archive-date=7 April 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170407144724/http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2008/partystatus.html |url-status=live }}</ref> The Labour Party won the party vote by a large majority in every Māori electorate, meaning that the typical Māori voter had split their vote, voting for a Māori Party candidate with their electorate vote and the Labour Party with their party vote.<ref>See Māori electorate results at [http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2008/electorateindex.html Chief Electoral Office: Official Count results: Electorate details] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090612040549/http://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2008/electorateindex.html |date=12 June 2009 }}.</ref>

The [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]] won the most seats overall and formed a [[minority government]] with the support of the Māori Party, [[ACT New Zealand]] and [[United Future]]. Sharples was given the [[Minister of Māori Affairs]] portfolio and became an Associate Minister of Corrections and Associate Minister of Education. Turia became Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector, Associate Minister of Health and Associate Minister for Social Development and Employment.<ref name="NZ_Herald_10543509">{{cite news |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10543509 |title=Key's Government |date=17 November 2008 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |access-date=19 October 2011 |archive-date=23 May 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110523074542/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10543509 |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Hone Harawira]] was critical of the alliance with the National Party and was suspended from the Māori Party in February 2011. He left the party and formed the left-wing [[Mana Movement|Mana Party]] in April 2011.<ref>Morgan Godfery, "Chapter 4.4: The Māori Party," pp. 246–247.</ref>

Competing against Mana, the Māori Party's strength diminished. In the [[2011 New Zealand general election|2011 general election]], it won only three electorates (with 1.43% of the party vote, the party was entitled to two seats, resulting in an [[overhang seat|overhang]] of one seat). The three MPs were [[Pita Sharples]] in [[Tāmaki Makaurau (New Zealand electorate)|Tāmaki Makaurau]], [[Tariana Turia]] in [[Te Tai Hauāuru]] and [[Te Ururoa Flavell]] in [[Waiāriki]]. [[Rahui Katene]] lost the Te Tai Tonga seat to [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour]]'s [[Rino Tirikatene]], and Hone Harawira won the [[Te Tai Tokerau]] seat for the Mana Party. The National Party again formed a [[minority government]] with the support of the Māori Party, ACT New Zealand and United Future. Sharples and Turia were returned as ministers outside cabinet. Ahead of the [[2014 New Zealand general election|2014 general election]], Flavell became the male co-leader. Neither Sharples nor Turia stood for re-election.<ref>Morgan Godfery, "Chapter 4.4: The Māori Party," pp. 247–248.</ref> At the election, Flavell held Waiāriki electorate seat, and the party was entitled to one further list seat as it received 1.32% of the party vote.<ref>{{cite web |title=New Zealand 2014 General Election Official Results |url=http://www.elections.org.nz/news-media/new-zealand-2014-general-election-official-results |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180613134004/http://www.elections.org.nz/news-media/new-zealand-2014-general-election-official-results |archive-date=13 June 2018 |access-date=8 October 2017 |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]]}}</ref> This went to [[Marama Fox]], who became the next female co-leader.{{citation needed|date=September 2024}}

Prior to the [[2017 New Zealand general election|2017 general election]], the Māori Party formed an electoral pact with the [[Mana Movement]] leader and former Māori Party MP [[Hone Harawira]]. The Māori Party agreed not to contest Te Tai Tokerau as part of a deal for the two parties to try to regain the [[Māori electorates]] from the Labour Party.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Moir |first1=Jo |title=Hone Harawira gets clear Te Tai Tokerau run for Mana not running against Maori Party in other seats |url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/89581527/hone-harawira-gets-clear-te-tai-tokerau-run-for-mana-not-running-against-maori-party-in-other-seats |access-date=7 October 2017 |newspaper=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=20 February 2017 |archive-date=11 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230411103725/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/89581527/hone-harawira-gets-clear-te-tai-tokerau-run-for-mana-not-running-against-maori-party-in-other-seats |url-status=live }}</ref> In the election, they failed to take any seats, with Labour capturing all seven of the Māori electorates.<ref name="2017 general election results" /><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/09/23/world/asia/new-zealand-election.html |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=23 September 2017 |quote=A major upset in Saturday's results was the vanquishing of the Maori Party, a group which grew out of protest action about indigenous rights to New Zealand's foreshore and seabed. Formed in 2004, the party won two seats at the 2014 election; in the next Parliament, it will have none. |title=Center-Right Party Hangs on in New Zealand Election |first=Charlotte |last=Graham |access-date=25 September 2017 |archive-date=25 September 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170925044915/https://www.nytimes.com/2017/09/23/world/asia/new-zealand-election.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Party co-leader [[Te Ururoa Flavell]] expressed sadness at the loss of seats and announced he would be resigning from politics.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Trevett |first1=Claire |title=Maori Party leader Te Ururoa Flavell leaving politics |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11925822 |access-date=7 October 2017 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=24 September 2017}}</ref> Fellow co-leader [[Marama Fox]] expressed bitterness at the party's defeat, remarking that New Zealand had chosen to return to the "age of colonization" and attacked the two major parties, National and Labour, for their alleged paternalism towards Māori.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Satherley |first1=Dan |title=NZ voted for return to "the age of colonisation" – Marama Fox |url=http://www.newshub.co.nz/home/shows/2017/09/nz-voted-for-return-to-the-age-of-colonisation-marama-fox.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170926154315/http://www.newshub.co.nz/home/shows/2017/09/nz-voted-for-return-to-the-age-of-colonisation-marama-fox.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=26 September 2017 |access-date=7 October 2017 |publisher=[[Newshub]] |date=24 September 2017}}</ref> Fox commented that Māori have "gone back like a beaten wife to the abuser" in regards to Labour's sweep of the Māori seats.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/97179049/mori-have-gone-back-like-a-beaten-wife-to-the-abuser-defiant-marama-fox-says |title=Māori have "gone back like a beaten wife to the abuser", defiant Marama Fox says |website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |access-date=18 April 2018 |archive-date=7 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180707010059/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/97179049/mori-have-gone-back-like-a-beaten-wife-to-the-abuser-defiant-marama-fox-says |url-status=live }}</ref> ''Metro Magazine'' described the Māori Party's poor results as being part of backlash against them for helping National form a government.<ref name="auto2" />  Within the following 12 months, the party's senior figures resigned: Flavell and Fox stepped down from the co-leadership and party president [[Tukoroirangi Morgan]] also resigned. This opened the field for a new generation of party leaders, namely [[Rawiri Waititi|Rāwiri Waititi]] and [[Debbie Ngarewa-Packer]].{{citation needed|date=September 2024}}

=== 2020 general election ===

The party announced [[John Tamihere]] as its candidate for the [[Tāmaki Makaurau (New Zealand electorate)|Tāmaki Makaurau]] electorate in March 2020. Tamihere had held the electorate from 2002 to 2005, but for the Labour Party. He had also run for [[Mayor of Auckland]] in [[2019 Auckland mayoral election|2019]] without success.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/411100/john-tamihere-to-run-for-maori-party-in-tamaki-makaurau |title=John Tamihere to run for Māori Party in Tāmaki Makaurau |date=6 March 2020 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |language=en-nz |access-date=9 March 2020 |archive-date=6 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200306122804/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/411100/john-tamihere-to-run-for-maori-party-in-tamaki-makaurau |url-status=live }}</ref> Tamihere's mayoral campaign was more right-wing, and he said the Māori Party could happily work with the National Party. This contradicted Māori Party President Che Wilson, who had set out a clear preference to work with Labour and had said "if we ever do talk to National it will have to be a big deal for us to move that way again."<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/411288/power-play-maori-party-strategy-already-undermined-by-tamihere |title=Power play: Māori Party strategy already undermined by Tamihere |date=9 March 2020 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |language=en-nz |access-date=9 March 2020 |archive-date=10 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200310151500/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/411288/power-play-maori-party-strategy-already-undermined-by-tamihere |url-status=live }}</ref>

On 15 April 2020, the party announced that John Tamihere and [[Debbie Ngarewa-Packer]] were the new party co-leaders.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/120911726/john-tamihere-and-debbie-ngarewapacker-selected-as-new-mori-party-coleaders |title=John Tamihere and Debbie Ngarewa-Packer selected as new Māori Party co-leaders |last=Forbes |first=Stephen |date=15 April 2020 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |language=en |access-date=15 April 2020 |archive-date=21 April 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200421030335/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/120911726/john-tamihere-and-debbie-ngarewapacker-selected-as-new-mori-party-coleaders |url-status=live }}</ref>

In late May 2020, the party received a broadcasting allocation of $145,101 for the [[2020 New Zealand general election|2020 election]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2020/2020-broadcasting-allocation-decision-released/ |title=2020 Broadcasting Allocation Decision Released |publisher=Electoral Commission |date=29 May 2020 |access-date=29 May 2020 |archive-date=6 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200806213409/https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2020/2020-broadcasting-allocation-decision-released/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In September 2020, [[Ikaroa-Rāwhiti]] candidate Heather Te Au-Skipworth released the party's sports policy which included establishing a national Māori sporting body and investing in Māori sporting scholarships and programs. She also stated "it is a known fact that Māori genetic makeup is stronger than others... Our ancestors were not just athletic, they were also strategic thinkers with intentions to survive. This all required stamina, resilience, endurance, speed, agility and logic."<ref>{{cite news |title=Funding promised for Maori sport |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/northland-age/news/funding-promised-for-maori-sport/C3MD4AZ2FG5F2RQVHPELSOLIAE/ |access-date=27 March 2024 |work=[[Northland Age]] |date=3 September 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240210231346/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/northland-age/news/funding-promised-for-maori-sport/C3MD4AZ2FG5F2RQVHPELSOLIAE/ |archive-date=10 February 2024}}</ref> The genetic superiority remarks were subsequently deleted prior to the [[2023 New Zealand general election]].<ref name="TVNZ Sep 2023">{{cite news |title=Q + A with Jack Tame – Rawiri Waiti: Maori health, Te Tiriti, and Parliament suspension |url=https://www.tvnz.co.nz/shows/q-and-a/clips/rawiri-waititi-m-ori-health-te-tiriti-and-parliament-suspension |access-date=26 March 2024 |work=[[TVNZ]] |date=10 September 2023}}</ref><ref name="CLM Sep 2023">{{cite web |last1=Lynch |first1=Chris |title=Te Pāti Māori co-leader Rawiri Waititi defends deleted racist comments |url=https://www.chrislynchmedia.com/news-items/te-pti-mori-co-leader-rawiri-waititi-defends-deleted-racist-comments |publisher=Chris Lynch Media |access-date=26 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231028042338/https://www.chrislynchmedia.com/news-items/te-pti-mori-co-leader-rawiri-waititi-defends-deleted-racist-comments |archive-date=28 October 2023 |date=10 September 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref>

At the 2020 general election, held in October, the Māori Party's [[Rawiri Waititi]] captured the [[Waiariki (New Zealand electorate)|Waiariki electorate]], defeating Labour MP [[Tāmati Coffey]] by a margin of 836 votes. This allowed the Māori Party to enter Parliament, and with its party vote of 1.2%, it was entitled to two MPs.<ref name="results2020">{{cite web |date=6 November 2020 |title=2020 General Election and Referendums – Official Result |url=https://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230621001306/https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=21 June 2023 |access-date=6 November 2020 |website=Electoral Commission}}</ref> After Waititi, Ngarewa-Packer entered Parliament as the highest-ranked person on the party list.<ref name="RNZ 6 Nov 2020">{{Cite news |title=Special votes: National loses two MPs, one each to Labour, Māori Party |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/430006/special-votes-national-loses-two-mps-one-each-to-labour-maori-party |access-date=6 November 2020 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=6 November 2020 |language=en-nz |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201106082134/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/430006/special-votes-national-loses-two-mps-one-each-to-labour-maori-party |archive-date=6 November 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref> As the only male Māori Party MP, Waititi replaced Tamihere as a co-leader.<ref>{{cite web |date=29 October 2020 |title=Māori Party's Rawiri Waititi replaces John Tamihere as co-leader |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/429357/maori-party-s-rawiri-waititi-replaces-john-tamihere-as-co-leader |access-date=29 October 2020 |publisher=[[RNZ]] |archive-date=1 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201101083903/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/429357/maori-party-s-rawiri-waititi-replaces-john-tamihere-as-co-leader |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite tweet |number=1317563765064282112 |user=KiwiPoll |title=John Tamihere confirms that Rawiri Waititi will take over the co-leadership. #MaoriPol #nzpol #Decision20 #YourVote2020 |date=17 October 2020 |access-date=19 October 2020 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20201019101218/https://twitter.com/KiwiPoll/status/1317563765064282112 |archive-date=19 October 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=NZ Election 2020: Waiariki's Rawiri Waititi will become Māori Party co-leader |url=https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2020/10/nz-election-2020-waiariki-s-rawiri-waititi-will-become-m-ori-party-co-leader.html |access-date=19 October 2020 |work=[[Newshub]] |date=19 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201019050144/https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2020/10/nz-election-2020-waiariki-s-rawiri-waititi-will-become-m-ori-party-co-leader.html |archive-date=19 October 2020 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

On 11 November, former party co-leader Tamihere requested a vote recount in the [[Māori electorates]] of [[Tāmaki Makaurau (New Zealand electorate)|Tāmaki Makaurau]] and [[Te Tai Hauāuru]], alleging Māori voters had encountered discrimination during the 2020 election. Tamihere claimed that the recount was intended to expose discriminatory laws such as the five-yearly Māori Electoral Option (which limited the ability of Māori to switch between the general and Māori rolls for a period five years). He also alleged longer wait times for Māori voters at election booths and some Māori not being allowed to vote on the Māori roll.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Burrows |first1=Matt |title=NZ Election 2020: Māori Party asks for recount in two electorates, pushes for Electoral Act reform |url=https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2020/11/nz-election-2020-m-ori-party-asks-for-recount-in-two-electorates-pushes-for-electoral-act-reform.amp.html |access-date=13 November 2020 |work=[[Newshub]] |date=13 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201113075414/https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2020/11/nz-election-2020-m-ori-party-asks-for-recount-in-two-electorates-pushes-for-electoral-act-reform.amp.html |archive-date=13 November 2020 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

=== 2020–2023 parliamentary term ===

On 26 November 2020, Te Pāti Māori MPs Waititi and Ngarewa-Packer walked out of Parliament after the [[Speaker of the New Zealand House of Representatives|Speaker of the House]] [[Trevor Mallard]] would not allow them to speak due to parliamentary procedures limiting the speaking time by smaller parties. Waititi had attempted to pass a motion that their party leaders be allowed to give a 15-minute "address in reply" but Mallard had blocked the motion on the grounds that MPs from smaller parties were not scheduled to give their maiden speeches until the following week. Waititi described Mallard's decision as unfair while Ngarewa-Packer claimed that this was "another example of the Māori voice being silenced and ignored."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Patterson |first1=Jane |title=Māori Party MPs walk out of Parliament in protest |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/431521/maori-party-mps-walk-out-of-parliament-in-protest |access-date=5 December 2020 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=26 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201129230930/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/431521/maori-party-mps-walk-out-of-parliament-in-protest |archive-date=29 November 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref>

==== 2020 election donations investigation ====

On 12 April 2021, the [[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]] referred Te Pāti Māori to the Police for failing to disclose about NZ$320,000 worth of donations within the required timeframe. These donations came from several individuals and organisations including former party co-leader Tamihere (NZ$158,223.72), the Urban Māori Authority (NZ$48,879.85), and the Aotearoa Te Kahu Limited Partnership (NZ$120,000). Party President Che Wilson attributed the late disclosure to the fact that the party was staffed by volunteers and rookies who were unfamiliar with electoral finance laws.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Trevett |first1=Claire |title=Election donations: Māori Party referred to police over $320,000 in undeclared donations |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/election-donations-maori-party-referred-to-police-over-320000-in-undeclared-donations/6ZHXNU36DJ6ZFJTP7E6J3GI5BY/ |access-date=12 April 2021 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=12 April 2021 |archive-date=12 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210412021429/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/election-donations-maori-party-referred-to-police-over-320000-in-undeclared-donations/6ZHXNU36DJ6ZFJTP7E6J3GI5BY/ |url-status=live }}</ref> On 29 April, the Police referred the investigation into the Māori Party's undeclared donations to the [[Serious Fraud Office (New Zealand)|Serious Fraud Office]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Manch |first1=Thomas |title=Police refer Māori Party to Serious Fraud Office over $328,000 in undeclared donations |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/124974834/police-refer-mori-party-to-serious-fraud-office-over-328000-in-undeclared-donations |access-date=29 April 2021 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=29 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428072105/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/124974834/police-refer-mori-party-to-serious-fraud-office-over-328000-in-undeclared-donations |archive-date=28 April 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref> By late September 2022, the Serious Fraud Office had closed the investigation and decided not to pursue prosecutions against the individuals and parties involved.<ref name="Bryce Edwards 30 Sep 2022">{{cite web |last1=Edwards |first1=Bryce |title=Political Roundup: Te Pāti Māori and vested interests |url=https://democracyproject.nz/2022/09/30/bryce-edwards-political-roundup-te-pati-maori-and-vested-interests/ |website=Democracy Project |publisher=[[Victoria University of Wellington]] |access-date=5 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220930001523/https://democracyproject.nz/2022/09/30/bryce-edwards-political-roundup-te-pati-maori-and-vested-interests/ |archive-date=30 September 2022 |date=30 September 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In late September 2022, [[Charities Services]] general manager Natasha Weight confirmed that the agency was investigating two charities headed by Party President Tamihere, the [[Te Whānau Waipareira Trust]] and the [[National Urban Māori Authority]], for financing his 2020 election campaign. According to the Charities Register, Te Whānau o Waipareira Trust Group had loaned Tamihere NZ$385,307 to support his 2020 election campaign while the National Urban Māori Authority had paid NZ$82,695 to support his 2020 election campaign and Te Pāti Māori aspirations. Under existing legislation, charities are not allowed to donate and endorse political parties and candidates or allow them to use a charity's resources. In response, Tamihere accused the Charities Services of discriminating against Te Pāti Māori and Māori causes. Tamihere and Te Pāti Māori also confirmed that they would litigate against the Charities Service if the agency ruled against them.<ref>{{cite news |last1=McConnell |first1=Glenn |last2=Piper |first2=Denise |title=John Tamihere defends his charities' payments and loans to his political campaigns |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/130008768/john-tamihere-defends-his-charities-payments-and-loans-to-his-political-campaigns |access-date=29 September 2022 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=28 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220928011602/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/130008768/john-tamihere-defends-his-charities-payments-and-loans-to-his-political-campaigns |archive-date=28 September 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Dine |first1=Jonty |title=Te Pāti Māori president claims party "demonised" by political donations investigation |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/475680/te-pati-maori-president-claims-party-demonised-by-political-donations-investigation |access-date=29 September 2022 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=28 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220928071526/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/475680/te-pati-maori-president-claims-party-demonised-by-political-donations-investigation |archive-date=28 September 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Tamihere |first1=John |title=Tamihere responds to NZ Herald allegations |url=https://waateanews.com/2022/09/28/john-tamihere-3/ |access-date=29 September 2022 |work=[[Waatea News]] |date=28 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220928040542/https://waateanews.com/2022/09/28/john-tamihere-3/ |archive-date=28 September 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref> Tamihere also criticised ''[[The New Zealand Herald]]'' journalist Matt Nippert's coverage of the two charities' donations to his campaigns, accusing the newspaper of racism and announcing that Te Pāti Māori would boycott the ''Herald''.<ref name="Bryce Edwards 30 Sep 2022" />

==== Hate Speech Task Force, 2021 ====

In June 2021, Te Pāti Māori called for a joint task force between the [[New Zealand Security Intelligence Service]] and [[New Zealand Police]] targeting right-wing extremists and rising anti-Māori [[hate speech]] in response to a [[YouTube]] video featuring a masked man calling for the slaughter of Māori and for a civil war. The video was later removed by YouTube for a breach of its community guidelines.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Call for taskforce targeting right-wing extremists with rise in anti-Māori talk |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/crime/125317785/call-for-taskforce-targeting-rightwing-extremists-with-rise-in-antimori-talk |date=2 June 2021 |access-date=8 June 2021 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210813231744/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/crime/125317785/call-for-taskforce-targeting-rightwing-extremists-with-rise-in-antimori-talk |archive-date=13 August 2021 |language=en}}</ref> In a tweet, the party said that the video contained threats against its MPs, [[marae]] and Māori.<ref>{{cite tweet |number=1399918936343269382 |user=Maori_Party |title=Following violent online threats which targeted our MP's, marae and te iwi Māori, Te Pāti Māori have called for the... |access-date=8 June 2021 |language=en |date=2 June 2021}}</ref> Police arrested a man after receiving multiple complaints about the video and a day after Te Pāti Māori laid a complaint with the [[Independent Police Conduct Authority]] (IPCA).<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |title=Arrest made over online death threat video that prompted Te Pāti Māori complaints |language=en |work=[[Newshub]] |url=https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/new-zealand/2021/06/arrest-made-over-online-death-threat-video-that-prompted-te-p-ti-m-ori-complaints.html |date=3 June 2021 |access-date=8 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210610033854/https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/new-zealand/2021/06/arrest-made-over-online-death-threat-video-that-prompted-te-p-ti-m-ori-complaints.html |archive-date=10 June 2021 |url-status=dead}}</ref> A 44-year-old male was charged with making an objectionable publication.<ref name=":2" />

In the complaint to the IPCA, the party accused the police of having double standards when dealing with death threats made against [[Pākehā]] and Māori.<ref name="Newshub 2 June 2021">{{Cite news |title=Māori Party lay complaint over police investigation into white supremacist video |language=en |work=[[Newshub]] |url=https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2021/06/m-ori-party-lay-complaint-over-police-investigation-into-white-supremacist-video.html |date=10 June 2021 |access-date=8 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210610033847/https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2021/06/m-ori-party-lay-complaint-over-police-investigation-into-white-supremacist-video.html |archive-date=10 June 2021 |url-status=dead}}</ref> It compared the police's response to the video with the treatment of those who made death threats against National MP [[Simeon Brown#Member of Parliament|Simeon Brown]].<ref name="Newshub 2 June 2021" /> Ngarewa-Packer stated, "Communication and response time was inadequate, the police have continued to minimise the nature of the threat against us and our people".<ref name="Newshub 2 June 2021" />

==== Racial discrimination ====

On 29 August 2023, Te Pāti Māori made a series of tweets apologising to refugee and migrant communities for "harmful narratives" of "xenophobia and racism" on their official party website.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |date=29 August 2023 |title=Te Pāti Māori apologises to refugees and migrant communities for 'harmful narratives' |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/496840/te-pati-maori-apologises-to-refugees-and-migrant-communities-for-harmful-narratives |access-date=28 October 2023 |website=[[RNZ]] |language=en-nz}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite web |date=28 October 2023 |title=Te Pāti Māori apologises for 'harmful narratives' about refugees and migrants on party website |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/kahu/election-2023-te-pati-maori-apologises-to-refugees-and-migrant-communities-for-harmful-narratives/GGMAAWV4NJAHTPKDGYOZIWHX7E/ |access-date=28 October 2023 |website=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |language=en-NZ |archive-date=28 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231028042337/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/kahu/election-2023-te-pati-maori-apologises-to-refugees-and-migrant-communities-for-harmful-narratives/GGMAAWV4NJAHTPKDGYOZIWHX7E/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Te Pāti Māori said they had removed words for their website and was rewriting policy documents. An example of policy rewriting included the "Indigenous First" framework in the party's Whānau Build policy.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":8" /> The policy indicated the intent to place Māori housing needs before all others.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":8" /> In 2022, Te Pāti Māori also removed a reference from its sports policy that claimed Māori genetic makeup was stronger than others.<ref name=":8" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=26 January 2022 |title=Māori Sports – MāoriParty2021 |url=https://www.maoriparty.org.nz/maori_sports |access-date=30 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220126170231/https://www.maoriparty.org.nz/maori_sports |archive-date=26 January 2022}}</ref>

==== Whaitiri joins party ====

On 3 May 2023, sitting minister [[Meka Whaitiri]] announced that she had left the Labour Party to join Te Pāti Māori. [[Speaker of the New Zealand House of Representatives|Speaker of the House]] [[Adrian Rurawhe]] confirmed that Whaitiri would serve the remainder of her 2020–2023 term as an independent member of Parliament under standing order 35(5), which avoids invoking the "[[waka-jumping]]" provisions of the [[Electoral (Integrity) Amendment Act 2018]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Palmer |first1=Russell |title=Speaker rules Meka Whaitiri not affected by 'waka-jumping' law |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/489210/speaker-rules-meka-whaitiri-not-affected-by-waka-jumping-law |access-date=4 May 2023 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=3 May 2023 |archive-date=3 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230503120212/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/489210/speaker-rules-meka-whaitiri-not-affected-by-waka-jumping-law |url-status=live }}</ref> Whaitiri does not sit with her party in Parliament. She will recontest the [[Ikaroa-Rāwhiti]] electorate as a Māori Party candidate.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Milne |first1=Jonathan |title=Minister Meka Whaitiri quits Govt to become Te Pāti Māori's first big-name election candidate |url=https://www.newsroom.co.nz/minister-meka-whaitiri-quits-govt-to-become-te-pati-maoris-first-big-name-election-candidate |access-date=4 May 2023 |work=Newsroom |date=3 May 2023 |language=en-NZ |archive-date=3 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230503110006/https://www.newsroom.co.nz/minister-meka-whaitiri-quits-govt-to-become-te-pati-maoris-first-big-name-election-candidate |url-status=live }}</ref>

On 10 May, Ngarewa-Packer and Waititi held a [[haka]] (dance) during Parliamentary proceedings to welcome Whaitiri to the Māori Party. In response, Rurawhe ordered Ngarewa-Packer and Waititi to leave Parliament since they had not obtained the permission of the Speaker or other parliamentary parties to hold the haka.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Palmer |first1=Russell |title=Whaitiri decries 'censure' after Te Pāti Māori leaders ejected from Parliament |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/489570/whaitiri-decries-censure-after-te-pati-maori-leaders-ejected-from-parliament |access-date=11 May 2023 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=9 May 2023 |archive-date=11 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230511012933/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/489570/whaitiri-decries-censure-after-te-pati-maori-leaders-ejected-from-parliament |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Speaker blunts celebration of Meka defection |url=https://waateanews.com/2023/05/10/speaker-blunts-celebration-of-meka-defection/ |access-date=11 May 2023 |work=Waatea News.com |publisher=[[Radio Waatea|Waatea News]] |date=10 May 2023 |archive-date=11 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230511013114/https://waateanews.com/2023/05/10/speaker-blunts-celebration-of-meka-defection/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== Name change ====

The party registered its current name, Te Pāti Māori, with the [[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]] on 12 July 2023, replacing its previous name, the Māori Party.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2023/change-to-te-pati-maori-party-name/ |title=Change to Te Pāti Māori party name |date=19 July 2023 |work=Electoral Commission New Zealand |access-date=19 July 2023 |archive-date=19 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230719014747/https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2023/change-to-te-pati-maori-party-name/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== 2023 election ===

Te Pāti Māori launched its [[2023 New Zealand general election|2023 general election]] campaign at Te Whānau O Waipareira's [[Matariki]] event in [[Henderson, New Zealand|Henderson]], Auckland on 14 July. The party campaigned on advancing the interests of the [[Māori people]], [[anti-racism|combating racism]], and the "second-rate" status of Māori, as Ngarewa-Packer labelled it.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Scott |first1=Matthew |title=Te Pāti Māori kicks off campaign with Matariki block party |url=https://www.newsroom.co.nz/te-pati-maori-kicks-off-campaign-with-matariki-block-party |access-date=16 July 2023 |work=[[Newsroom (website)|Newsroom]] |date=14 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230727101739/https://www.newsroom.co.nz/te-pati-maori-kicks-off-campaign-with-matariki-block-party |archive-date=27 July 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref>

On 27 July, the party announced several redistributive tax policies including a zero tax policy on those earning below NZ$30,000, a new 48% tax on those earning above NZ$300,000, raising the companies tax rate back to 33% and a wealth tax on millionaires.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Neilson |first1=Michael |title=Māori Party wealth tax plan: Over 98 per cent of NZers get tax cut, GST off kai and higher top rates |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/maori-party-wealth-tax-plan-over-98-per-cent-of-nzers-get-tax-cut-gst-off-kai-and-higher-top-rates/YEMJJZGV2ZFX5DJG5MFVDDRLQM/ |access-date=2 August 2023 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=27 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230731221416/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/maori-party-wealth-tax-plan-over-98-per-cent-of-nzers-get-tax-cut-gst-off-kai-and-higher-top-rates/YEMJJZGV2ZFX5DJG5MFVDDRLQM/ |archive-date=31 July 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Palmer |first1=Russell |title=Te Pāti Māori proposes suite of changes in new tax policies |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/494586/te-pati-maori-proposes-suite-of-changes-in-new-tax-policies |access-date=2 August 2023 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=27 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230729202312/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/494586/te-pati-maori-proposes-suite-of-changes-in-new-tax-policies |archive-date=29 July 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref> On 2 August, the party campaigned on ending state care for Māori children and replacing the present [[Oranga Tamariki]] (Ministry for Children) with an independent [[Mokopuna Māori Authority]] that would network with Māori organisations, [[iwi]] (tribes), and [[hapū]] (sub-groups) to ensure that Māori children remained connected with their [[whakapapa]] (genealogies).<ref>{{cite news |last1=Neilson |first1=Michael |title=Election 2023: Māori Party vows to take Māori children out of state care, replace Oranga Tamariki with Mokopuna Māori Authority |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/election-2023-maori-party-vows-to-take-maori-children-out-of-state-care-replace-oranga-tamariki-with-mokopuna-maori-authority/FMU36AAYIVFJRB2EPISCPSCYSU/ |access-date=2 August 2023 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=2 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230802024108/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/election-2023-maori-party-vows-to-take-maori-children-out-of-state-care-replace-oranga-tamariki-with-mokopuna-maori-authority/FMU36AAYIVFJRB2EPISCPSCYSU/ |archive-date=2 August 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In late August 2023, Te Pāti Māori revised its Whanau Build (housing) policy to eliminate an "indigenous first" provision which called for immigration to be curbed until the country's housing supply was addressed. The party also apologised to migrant and refugee communities for promoting what it described as "harmful narratives" on its website, and reiterated that it would treat everyone like how they would be treated as guests on a [[marae]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Dexter |first1=Giles |title=Election 2023: Te Pati Maori apologised to refugees and migrant communities for 'harmful narratives' on party websites |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/kahu/election-2023-te-pati-maori-apologises-to-refugees-and-migrant-communities-for-harmful-narratives/GGMAAWV4NJAHTPKDGYOZIWHX7E/ |access-date=26 March 2024 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=29 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240121124658/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/kahu/election-2023-te-pati-maori-apologises-to-refugees-and-migrant-communities-for-harmful-narratives/GGMAAWV4NJAHTPKDGYOZIWHX7E/ |archive-date=21 January 2024}}</ref>

During an interview with [[TVNZ]] journalist [[Jack Tame]] in September 2023, Waititi also denied that his party's sports policy' comments about "Māori genetic makeup being stronger than others" were racist. These comments were subsequently deleted from Te Pāti Māori's website. When challenged by Tame, he responded that TPM was "trying to empower people that are climbing out from the bottom of the bonnet of colonial violence for the last 193 years" by encouraging pride in their heritage.<ref name="TVNZ Sep 2023" /><ref name="CLM Sep 2023" />

Te Pāti Māori won six electorate seats and 3.08% of the popular vote.<ref name="2023 results" /> Meka Whaitiri stood as the party's candidate in the [[Ikaroa-Rāwhiti]] electorate but was defeated by Labour's candidate [[Cushla Tangaere-Manuel]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Ikaroa-Rawhiti – Official Result |url=https://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-67.html |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]] |date=3 November 2023 |access-date=26 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231123104119/https://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-67.html |archive-date=23 November 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref> Despite Whaitiri's [[unseating]], the 2023 election outcome was Te Pāti Māori's most successful election result.<ref name="RNZ 21 Dec 2023">{{cite news |last1=Dexter |first1=Giles |title=Te Pāti Māori plans for future as it reflects on success in Māori seats |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/focusonpolitics/audio/2018915647/te-pati-maori-plans-for-future-as-it-reflects-on-success-in-maori-seats |access-date=21 December 2023 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=18 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231120160902/https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/focusonpolitics/audio/2018915647/te-pati-maori-plans-for-future-as-it-reflects-on-success-in-maori-seats |archive-date=20 November 2023}}</ref>

==== 2023 election data breach allegations ====
On 2 June 2024, the ''[[Sunday Star Times]]'' journalist [[Andrea Vance]] reported that [[Statistics New Zealand]] was investigating allegations by former staff at Manurewa Marae that Te Pāti Māori had illegally used [[2023 New Zealand census]] data to target [[Māori electorates|Māori electorate]] voters in the [[Tāmaki Makaurau (New Zealand electorate)|Tāmaki Makaurau]] electorate during the 2023 election, and that participants were given supermarket vouchers, wellness packs and food parcels to encourage them to fill out census forms and switch to the Māori electoral roll. Te Pāti Māori's candidate [[Takutai Tarsh Kemp]] had won the Tāmaki Makaurau electorate during the 2023 general election. A whistleblower from the [[Ministry of Social Development (New Zealand)|Ministry of Social Development]] (MSD) had alerted Statistics NZ and the Police. In response, Te Pāti Māori leader Tamihere denied the allegations and claimed that they were made by disgruntled former staff. Tamihere said that the marae had been working with the Whānau Ora Commissioning Agency to promote Māori participation in the 2023 census. Tamihere also acknowledged that marae workers had given gifts to encourage people to participate in the 2023 Census and switch to the Māori roll but denied allegations of wrongdoing.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Vance |first1=Andrea |title=Stats NZ investigating potential misuse of Māori census data |url=https://www.thepost.co.nz/politics/350293431/stats-nz-investigating-potential-misuse-maori-census-data |access-date=3 June 2024 |work=[[The Post (New Zealand newspaper)|The Post]] |date=2 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240601195140/https://www.thepost.co.nz/politics/350293431/stats-nz-investigating-potential-misuse-maori-census-data |archive-date=1 June 2024}}</ref>

On 5 June, Vance reported that the [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour Party]] had filed a complaint against Te Pāti Māori in November 2023 for allegedly using personal information collected during the COVID-19 immunisation programme for political campaigning purposes during the 2023 election, which constitutes a breach of electoral law. Labour's complaint alleged that Māori voters in Auckland had received two text messages from the text code 2661 urging them to vote for Te Pāti Māori. 2661 was registered with the Waipareira Trust, which is led by TPM's President Tamihere.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Vance |first1=Andrea |title=Complaint alleged Te Pāti Māori misused info collected for Covid vaccination drive |url=https://www.thepost.co.nz/politics/350299612/complaint-alleged-te-pati-maori-misused-info-collected-covid-vaccination-drive |access-date=7 June 2024 |work=[[The Post (New Zealand newspaper)|The Post]] |date=5 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240604233828/https://www.thepost.co.nz/politics/350299612/complaint-alleged-te-pati-maori-misused-info-collected-covid-vaccination-drive |archive-date=4 June 2024}}</ref> In response, Labour leader [[Chris Hipkins]], [[ACT New Zealand]] leader [[David Seymour]], Prime Minister and [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]] leader [[Christopher Luxon]] called for an investigation into the allegations against TPM.<ref name="NZH Hipkins Jun 2024">{{cite news |title=Labour leader Chris Hipkins says Te Pāti Māori allegations very serious |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/te-pati-maori-unequivocally-refutes-claims-manurewa-marae-misused-census-data/7QKVPX2DIZAMJDA3AE64OZS6WA/ |access-date=7 June 2024 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=5 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240606072112/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/te-pati-maori-unequivocally-refutes-claims-manurewa-marae-misused-census-data/7QKVPX2DIZAMJDA3AE64OZS6WA/ |archive-date=6 June 2024}}</ref><ref name="NZH Luxon Jun 2024">{{cite news |last1=Maher |first1=Rachel |last2=Trevett |first2=Claire |last3=Gabel |first3=Julia |title=PM Christopher Luxon calls Te Pāti Māori Census allegations 'pretty concerning', Stats NZ launches investigation |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/pm-christopher-luxon-calls-te-pati-maori-census-allegations-pretty-concerning-stats-nz-launches-investigation/XX65HCEUURCCRFXFHWT3ICC2YA/ |access-date=7 June 2024 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=6 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240605210850/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/pm-christopher-luxon-calls-te-pati-maori-census-allegations-pretty-concerning-stats-nz-launches-investigation/XX65HCEUURCCRFXFHWT3ICC2YA/ |archive-date=5 June 2024}}</ref> The [[Privacy Commissioner (New Zealand)|Privacy Commissioner]] also confirmed that Statistics NZ had alerted it to a potential privacy breach during its investigation. Chief statistician Mark Sowden also called for anyone with information to contact Statistics NZ.<ref name="NZH Luxon Jun 2024" /> In response to the second allegations, Tamihere issued a press release denouncing the allegations as baseless and claiming that the party was being targeted by opponents for speaking up for Māori. Tamihere also accused [[Destiny Church (New Zealand)|Destiny Church]] leader [[Brian Tamaki]] and his followers of attempting to take over Manurewa Marae.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Tamihere |first1=John |title=From The Party President – 'Naughty Natives Are At It Again' |url=https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PO2406/S00028/from-the-party-president-naughty-natives-are-at-it-again.htm |website=[[Scoop (website)|Scoop]] |access-date=7 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240606123413/https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PO2406/S00028/from-the-party-president-naughty-natives-are-at-it-again.htm |archive-date=6 June 2024 |date=6 June 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

On 7 June, co-leaders Waititi and Ngarewa-Packer called for an urgent Police investigation into the data breach allegations made against Te Pāti Māori. Police confirmed they were already investigating complaints they had received.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gabel |first1=Julia |title=Manurewa Marae data misuse claims: Te Pāti Māori ask police, Prime Minister for urgent investigation into 'frivolous' allegations |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/te-pati-maori-asks-prime-minister-for-urgent-investigation-into-frivolous-allegations/35QKL5PQOVCFPB22SJTR2BWWEE/ |access-date=9 June 2024 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=7 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240607185045/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/te-pati-maori-asks-prime-minister-for-urgent-investigation-into-frivolous-allegations/35QKL5PQOVCFPB22SJTR2BWWEE/ |archive-date=7 June 2024}}</ref> That same day, acting [[Public Service Commission (New Zealand)|Public Service Commission]]er Heather Baggott convened a meeting with the heads of the Statistics New Zealand, the [[Ministry of Health (New Zealand)|Ministry of Health]], [[Te Whatu Ora]] (Health New Zealand), the Ministry of Social Development, the [[Ministry of Justice (New Zealand)|Ministry of Justice]], the [[Department of Internal Affairs]], [[Te Puni Kōkiri]] (Ministry for Māori Development), [[Oranga Tamariki]] (Ministry for Children) and the [[Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet (New Zealand)|Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet]], the [[New Zealand Police]] and Electoral Commission to ensure that all relevant agencies were investigating the data breach allegations<ref>{{cite news |title=Nine agency bosses meet over Te Pāti Māori data allegations |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/518949/nine-agency-bosses-meet-over-te-pati-maori-data-allegations |access-date=9 June 2024 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=7 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240607082033/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/518949/nine-agency-bosses-meet-over-te-pati-maori-data-allegations |archive-date=7 June 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

On 10 June 2024, Prime Minister Luxon announced that the [[Public Service Commission (New Zealand)|Public Service Commission]] would launch an independent inquiry into government agencies' safeguards for protecting people's personal data and the circumstances surrounding the data breach allegations against Te Pāti Māori. The party was not notified of the Commission's inquiry. Employment advocate Allan Hulse, who represented six former Manurewa Marae staff and the MSD employee, alleged that 1,400 census forms were photocopied and uploaded into a database owned by the Waiparera Trust. Hulse also alleged that staff used census data to help people transfer from the general to Māori roll. Tamihere has rejected these allegations, calling for people to produce "hard evidence."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Wilton |first1=Perry |title=Prime Minister Christopher Luxon announces Public Service Commission inquiry into Census data allegations linked to Te Pāti Māori |url=https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2024/06/prime-minister-christopher-luxon-announces-public-service-commission-inquiry-into-te-p-ti-m-ori-after-census-data-allegations.html |access-date=10 June 2024 |work=[[Newshub]] |date=10 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240610055122/https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2024/06/prime-minister-christopher-luxon-announces-public-service-commission-inquiry-into-te-p-ti-m-ori-after-census-data-allegations.html |archive-date=10 June 2024}}</ref>

In early July 2024, former Māori academic Rawiri Taonui disputed the allegations against Te Pāti Māori, the Waipareira Trust and Manurewa Marae; arguing that photocopies of census data were taken solely for verification purposes and destroyed, highlighting that Statistics New Zealand had clarified that neither Tamihera, the Waipareira Trust and the Whanau Ora Commissioning Agency had access to their database, disputing that vouchers were used to encourage people to switch to the Māori electoral roll, and denying that Māori Party flyers were included in wellbeing packs.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Taonui |first1=Rawiri |title=Data and Enrolment Allegations at Manurewa Marae |url=https://waateanews.com/2024/07/08/mataki-investigate-pre-election-data-and-enrolment-allegations-at-manurewa-marae/ |access-date=14 July 2024 |work=[[Radio Waatea|Waatea News]] |date=8 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240714091130/https://waateanews.com/2019/09/04/l-a-b-experiments-with-raw-sound-in-prize-mix/ |archive-date=14 July 2024}}</ref> In late August 2024, Taonui claimed that the whistleblowers were connected to Destiny Church and had instigated the allegations against Manurewa Marae and Te Pāti Māori following a failed attempt by the church to take over the marae.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Taonui |first1=Rawiri |title=Destiny Church behind allegations against Te Pāti Māori and Manurewa Marae |url=https://waateanews.com/2024/08/27/destiny-church-behind-allegations-against-te-pati-maori-and-manurewa-marae/ |publisher=[[Radio Waatea|Waatea News]] |access-date=22 January 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250119173705/https://waateanews.com/2024/08/27/destiny-church-behind-allegations-against-te-pati-maori-and-manurewa-marae/ |archive-date=19 January 2025 |date=27 August 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

On 22 January 2025, a Statistics New Zealand report cleared the Whanau Ora Commissioning Agency of data breaches during the 2023 Census, finding that the agency increased Māori participation. The report made nine recommendations to improve Statistics NZ's procedures and referred allegations against Manurewa Marae to the [[Privacy Commissioner (New Zealand)|Privacy Commissioner]]. The report also found no evidence that one of the alleged whistleblowers had attempted to contact Statistics NZ regarding allegations against the marae.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Los'e |first1=Joseph |title=Stats NZ inquiry clears Whānau Ora of 2023 Census data breach |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/stats-nz-inquiry-clears-whanau-ora-of-2023-census-data-breach/MSHXHJ7HUFGDLO3D7UEU54XWGI/ |access-date=22 January 2025 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=20 January 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250120013246/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/stats-nz-inquiry-clears-whanau-ora-of-2023-census-data-breach/MSHXHJ7HUFGDLO3D7UEU54XWGI/ |archive-date=20 January 2025}}</ref>

On 11 February 2025, ''The New Zealand Herald'' reported that Detective Superintendent Ross McKay was leading the inquiry into allegations regarding Te Pāti Māori's misuse of census data and Covid-19 vaccination information at Manurewa Marae for electoral campaigning purposes.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Los'e |first1=Joseph |title=Manurewa Marae data misuse claims: Top police detective Ross McKay leading investigation into Te Pāti Māori |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/kahu/manurewa-marae-data-misuse-claims-top-police-detective-ross-mckay-leading-investigation-into-te-pati-maori/KAW4JBMTNZGSHFMICNC6OGMXBA/ |access-date=13 February 2025 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=11 February 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250211173837/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/kahu/manurewa-marae-data-misuse-claims-top-police-detective-ross-mckay-leading-investigation-into-te-pati-maori/KAW4JBMTNZGSHFMICNC6OGMXBA/ |archive-date=11 February 2025}}</ref> On 2 October, the Police and [[Serious Fraud Office (New Zealand)|Serious Fraud Office]] (SFO) halted their investigation into the Manurewa Marae electoral misconduct allegations after they found insufficient evidence of corruption. The SFO and [[Privacy Commissioner (New Zealand)|Privacy Commissioner]] are still investigating potential privacy breaches.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Perese |first1=Daniel |title=Manurewa Marae avoids criminal probe after Police find no proof of corruption |url=https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2025/10/02/manurewa-marae-avoids-criminal-probe-after-police-find-no-proof-of-corruption/ |access-date=2 October 2025 |work=[[Te Ao Māori News]] |date=2 October 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251002231413/https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2025/10/02/manurewa-marae-avoids-criminal-probe-after-police-find-no-proof-of-corruption/ |archive-date=2 October 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== 2023–present: In opposition ===
Ngarewa Packer stated that the party would serve as "the only true opposition" in Parliament for the next term, adding that their plans were "to shake Parliament up and normalise it for Māori."<ref name="RNZ 21 Dec 2023" /> During the opening of  the [[54th New Zealand Parliament]] on 5 December 2023, Te Pāti Māori organised a series of nationwide protests known as the [[National Māori Action Day]] to protest against the [[Sixth National Government of New Zealand|National-led coalition government]]'s policies on [[co-governance]] and the Treaty of Waitangi.<ref>{{cite news |title=National Māori Action Day – Te Pāti Māori protests in pictures |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/503939/national-maori-action-day-te-pati-maori-protests-in-pictures |access-date=21 December 2023 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=5 December 2023 |archive-date=19 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231219130042/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/503939/national-maori-action-day-te-pati-maori-protests-in-pictures |url-status=live }}</ref> The party's MPs also modified their oaths of allegiances to reference the Treaty of Waitangi.<ref>{{cite news |title=Māori dissent sets the scene as Parliament returns |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/focusonpolitics/audio/2018918535/maori-dissent-sets-the-scene-as-parliament-returns |access-date=21 December 2023 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=8 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231216084423/https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/focusonpolitics/audio/2018918535/maori-dissent-sets-the-scene-as-parliament-returns |archive-date=16 December 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In late May 2024, Te Pāti Māori and the Toitu Te Tiriti movement called for a nationwide day of protest known as "Toitū Te Tiriti National Day of Action" to coincide with the release of the [[2024 New Zealand budget]] on 30 May. The protest was in opposition to the National-led government perceived assault on [[Tangata whenua]] and the [[Treaty of Waitangi]]. The party urged all Māori to go on strike and attend [[hīkoi]] (protests) near their location. Protest action includes a car convoy travelling from [[New Zealand State Highway 1|State Highway 1]] south of Auckland to [[Hamilton, New Zealand|Hamilton]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ruru |first1=Karanama |title=Māori, allies encouraged to go on strike as part of second 'nationwide activation' |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/nz-news/350291630/maori-allies-encouraged-go-strike-part-second-nationwide-activation |access-date=28 May 2024 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=27 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240527083228/https://www.stuff.co.nz/nz-news/350291630/maori-allies-encouraged-go-strike-part-second-nationwide-activation |archive-date=27 May 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Maher |first1=Rachel |title=Te Pāti Māori protest plans to cause major disruptions on Thursday |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/te-pati-maori-protest-plans-to-cause-major-traffic-disruptions-on-thursday/6MCP5V726FGCNFLB53I6PMQBR4/ |access-date=28 May 2024 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=28 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240527234836/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/te-pati-maori-protest-plans-to-cause-major-traffic-disruptions-on-thursday/6MCP5V726FGCNFLB53I6PMQBR4/ |archive-date=27 May 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> Te Pāti Māori claimed that 100,000 people attended the "car-koi activation" rallies nationwide and advocated the establishment of a Māori parliament.<ref name="devolution">{{cite news |last1=Paterson |first1=Te Aniwaniwa |title=Te Pāti Māori issues declaration to set up a Māori parliament |url=https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2024/05/30/te-pati-maori-issues-declaration-to-set-up-a-maori-parliament/ |access-date=30 May 2024 |work=Te Ao Māori News |publisher=[[Whakaata Māori]] |date=30 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240530220121/https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2024/05/30/te-pati-maori-issues-declaration-to-set-up-a-maori-parliament/ |archive-date=30 May 2024}}</ref>

On 14 November 2024, Te Pāti Māori  MP [[Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke]] along with co-leaders Waititi, Ngarewa-Packer and Labour MP [[Peeni Henare]] led a protest [[haka]] (''[[Ka Mate]]'') that disrupted vote proceedings during the first reading of [[ACT New Zealand|ACT party]] leader [[David Seymour]]'s contentious [[Treaty Principles Bill]]. On 10 December, the four were referred to Parliament's Privileges Committee for their disruptive actions.<ref>{{cite news |last1=McConnell |first1=Glenn |title='Do I care? No': Te Pāti Māori responds to Speaker's rebuke over haka |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360517484/te-pati-maori-and-labour-mps-referred-privileges-committee-over-haka |access-date=15 December 2024 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=10 December 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241213013738/https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360517484/te-pati-maori-and-labour-mps-referred-privileges-committee-over-haka |archive-date=13 December 2024|url-status=live}}</ref> In late March 2025, the Privileges Committee ruled that Henare had acted in a "disorderly" way in joining the TPM-led haka but ruled that his actions did not amount to "contempt."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hanly |first1=Lillian |title=Labour's Peeni Henare not in contempt over 'disorderly' actions during Treaty Principles reading |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/547574/labour-s-peeni-henare-not-in-contempt-over-disorderly-actions-during-treaty-principles-reading |access-date=4 April 2025 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=26 March 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250326151950/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/547574/labour-s-peeni-henare-not-in-contempt-over-disorderly-actions-during-treaty-principles-reading |archive-date=26 March 2025|url-status=live}}</ref> On 14 May 2025, the Committee found Maipi-Clarke, Waititi and Ngarewa-Packer in contempt of Parliament. Maipi-Clarke was suspended from Parliament for seven days while Waititi and Ngarewa-Packer were suspended for 21 days. Te Pāti denounced the suspensions as an attempt by colonial powers to intimidate Māori.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Burr |first1=Lloyd |title=Te Pati Maori receive 'harshest punishment Privileges Committee's ever handed out' |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360689225/te-pati-maori-receive-harshest-punishment-privileges-committees-ever-handed-out |access-date=14 May 2025 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=14 May 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250514095014/https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360689225/te-pati-maori-receive-harshest-punishment-privileges-committees-ever-handed-out |archive-date=14 May 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> On 5 June, Parliament voted to uphold the suspensions of the three TPM MPs. In response, the party denounced the suspensions with President John Tamihere announcing that the three suspended MPs would be embarking on a national tour to rally opposition against the Government's proposed [[Regulatory Standards Bill]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Dexter |first1=Giles |title=Suspended Te Pati Maori MPs to embark on a national tour |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/563318/suspended-te-pati-maori-mps-to-embark-on-national-tour |access-date=7 June 2025 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=6 June 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250606054558/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/563318/suspended-te-pati-maori-mps-to-embark-on-national-tour |archive-date=6 June 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>

On 4 February 2025, Waititi and Ngarewa-Packer proposed the creation of a Parliamentary Commissioner for [[Treaty of Waitangi|Te Tiriti o Waitangi]], who would have extraordinary powers to audit bills and issue a "Tiriti veto" if policy and bills did not comply with the Treaty.
