They said this would be a "bottomline" in any coalition negotiations during events leading up to [[Waitangi Day]] at the Treaty Grounds.<ref>{{cite news |last1=McConnell |first1=Glenn |title=Te Pāti Māori issues coalition ultimatum, naming Treaty Commissioner as a 'bottom line' |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360570421/te-pati-maori-issues-coalition-ultimatum-naming-treaty-commissioner-bottom-line |access-date=13 February 2025 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=4 February 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250213215804/https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360570421/te-pati-maori-issues-coalition-ultimatum-naming-treaty-commissioner-bottom-line |archive-date=13 February 2025}}</ref> In response, ACT leader Seymour accused Te Pāti Māori of attempting to "break democracy" and urged Labour leader [[Chris Hipkins]] to rule out such as policy. Hipkins said he would not support TPM's policy for a Te Tiriti Commissioner with the powers to overturn law but added he was open to ensuring there were better "checks and balances" in New Zealand's constitutional framework.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Witton |first1=Bridie |title=Te Pāti Māori's push for a Te Tiriti commissioner is 'unconstitutional' |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360571359/te-pati-maoris-push-te-tiriti-commissioner-unconstitutional |access-date=13 February 2025 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=5 February 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250208075756/https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360571359/te-pati-maoris-push-te-tiriti-commissioner-unconstitutional |archive-date=8 February 2025}}</ref>

On 10 April 2025, Te Pāti Māori announced that the party would be standing candidates in general seats at the [[2026 New Zealand general election]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Te Pāti Māori to run candidates in general seats at next election |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/557788/te-pati-maori-to-run-candidates-in-general-seats-at-next-election |access-date=10 April 2025 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=10 April 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250410234523/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/557788/te-pati-maori-to-run-candidates-in-general-seats-at-next-election |archive-date=10 April 2025|url-status=live}}</ref>

On 31 July 2025, the party filed urgent [[High Court of New Zealand|High Court]] proceedings calling on the Electoral Commission, [[Ministry of Justice (New Zealand)|Ministry of Justice]] and the Ombudsman to investigate allegations that Māori voters had been removed from the Māori electoral roll or shifted to the general roll without their consent.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Dunlop |first1=Māni |last2=Te Wake |first2=Whatitiri |last3=Molyneux |first3=Tini |title=Te Pāti Māori files urgent court action over alleged voter suppression |url=https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2025/07/31/te-pati-maori-files-urgent-court-action-over-alleged-voter-suppression/ |access-date=3 August 2025 |work=[[Te Ao Māori News]] |publisher=[[Whakaata Māori]] |date=31 July 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250803032121/https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2025/07/31/te-pati-maori-files-urgent-court-action-over-alleged-voter-suppression/ |archive-date=3 August 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>

On 6 September 2025, Te Pāti Māori's candidate and former broadcaster [[Oriini Kaipara]] won a [[landslide victory]] in the [[2025 Tāmaki Makaurau by-election]], retaining the [[Tāmaki Makaurau (electorate)|Tāmaki Makaurau]] electorate for the party.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Williams |first1=Caroline |last2=Burr |first2=Lloyd |date=6 September 2025 |title='Looking forward to fighting a good fight': Oriini Kaipara wins Tāmaki Makaurau by-election |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360815477/tamaki-makaurau-election-polling-closed-candidates-wait-results |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250906095422/https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360815477/tamaki-makaurau-election-polling-closed-candidates-wait-results |archive-date=6 September 2025 |access-date=6 September 2025 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Tāmaki Makaurau – Preliminary Count |url=https://electionresults.govt.nz/ |access-date=6 September 2025 |website=electionresults.govt.nz |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]]}}</ref> The Tāmaki Makaurau electorate had been vacated by the death of sitting TPM MP [[Takutai Tarsh Kemp]] on 26 June 2025.<ref name="x631">{{cite news |last=Gabel |first=Julia |date=30 June 2025 |title=Watch: 'We will miss her' – MP Takutai Tarsh Kemp to be laid to rest today |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/te-pati-maori-mp-takutai-tarsh-kemp-to-be-laid-to-rest-today/4SPVNTGAKFBINCQ7QWWFMALFNA/ |access-date=30 June 2025 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]}}</ref>

==== 2025–26 internal conflict ====
In mid-September 2025, the party's [[Te Tai Tokerau]] MP [[Mariameno Kapa-Kingi]] was replaced as [[Whip (politics)|party whip]] by co-leader [[Debbie Ngarewa-Packer]],<ref>{{Cite news |last=Ensor |first=Jamie |date=11 September 2025 |title=Te Pāti Māori MP Mariameno Kapa-Kingi removed as party whip by leadership, addresses Tākuta Ferris' post |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/te-pati-maori-mp-mariameno-kapa-kingi-removed-as-party-whip-by-leadership-addresses-takuta-ferris-post/ZAJBI6N7G5BCVNRSBMVE2HFWEE/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250911195425/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/te-pati-maori-mp-mariameno-kapa-kingi-removed-as-party-whip-by-leadership-addresses-takuta-ferris-post/ZAJBI6N7G5BCVNRSBMVE2HFWEE/ |archive-date=11 September 2025 |access-date=12 September 2025 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |language=en-NZ}}</ref> with party president [[John Tamihere]] alleging that Kapa-Kingi had become detached from her constituents.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Te Wake |first1=Whatitiri |date=12 September 2025 |title='Tākuta is sorting his act out as of today'– Te Pāti Māori President |url=https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2025/09/12/takuta-is-sorting-his-act-out-as-of-today-te-pati-maori-president/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250915011214/https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2025/09/12/takuta-is-sorting-his-act-out-as-of-today-te-pati-maori-president/ |archive-date=15 September 2025 |access-date=15 September 2025 |work=[[Te Ao Māori News]]}}</ref> On 2 October 2025, the Toitū Te Tiriti's leader [[Eru Kapa-Kingi]] – the son of Mariameno Kapa-Kingi – confirmed that the group would formally sever relations with Te Pāti Māori, citing concerns about alleged bullying, authoritarian leadership, a clash of values, and the need for independence. In response, Te Pāti Māori rejected allegations of bullying and authoritarian leadership, and claimed that its decision-making process was transparent and compliant with its constitution.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Dunlop |first1=Māni |title=Toitū Te Tiriti cuts ties with Te Pāti Māori |url=https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2025/10/02/toitu-te-tiriti-cuts-ties-with-te-pati-maori/ |access-date=2 October 2025 |work=[[Te Ao Māori News]] |date=2 October 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251002032313/https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2025/10/02/toitu-te-tiriti-cuts-ties-with-te-pati-maori/ |archive-date=2 October 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> On 9 October, the party's co-leaders announced plans to "reset" the party following internal conflict.<ref>{{cite news |last1=McConnell |first1=Glenn |title=Te Pati Maori reveals 'reset,' saying it warns to govern |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360849737/te-pati-maori-reveals-reset-saying-it-wants-govern |access-date=28 October 2025 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=9 October 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251009064503/https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360849737/te-pati-maori-reveals-reset-saying-it-wants-govern |archive-date=9 October 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> On 14 October, Te Pāti Māori circulated an internal email to its membership, alleging various indiscretions by both Eru and Mariameno Kapa-Kingi. The email alleged that Eru racially abused a parliamentary security guard, and that Mariameno failed to pay her staffers and exceeded her parliamentary office budget by NZ$133,000.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Pearse |first1=Adam |title=Te Pāti Māori's Mariameno Kapa-Kingi allegedly warned of $133k office overspend, urged to take action so staff paid – party emails claims about MP and her son to members |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/te-pati-maoris-mariameno-kapa-kingi-allegedly-warned-of-133k-office-overspend-urged-to-take-action-so-staff-paid-party-emails-claims-about-mp-and-her-high-profile-son-to-members/MO7W4PIYHBHKLLAKSWRHBABE5U/ |access-date=21 October 2025 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=14 October 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251021023728/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/te-pati-maoris-mariameno-kapa-kingi-allegedly-warned-of-133k-office-overspend-urged-to-take-action-so-staff-paid-party-emails-claims-about-mp-and-her-high-profile-son-to-members/MO7W4PIYHBHKLLAKSWRHBABE5U/|archive-date=21 October 2025|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Dunlop |first1=Mani |title=Analysis: Te Pāti Māori turmoil exposes a deeper hurt for Māori |url=https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2025/10/14/analysis-te-pati-maori-turmoil-exposes-a-deeper-hurt-for-maori/ |access-date=21 October 2025 |work=[[Te Ao Māori News]] |date=14 October 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251021024333/https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2025/10/14/analysis-te-pati-maori-turmoil-exposes-a-deeper-hurt-for-maori/|archive-date=21 October 2025|url-status=live}}</ref> In late October 2025, [[Radio Waatea|Waatea News]] reported that the party's membership had voted to recommend suspending Mariameno and "resetting" the party's Te Tai Tokerau electorate executive.<ref>{{cite news |title=Te Pati Māori MP faces suspension |url=https://waateanews.com/2025/10/27/te-pati-maori-mp-faces-suspension/ |access-date=28 October 2025 |work=[[Radio Waatea|Waatea News]] |date=27 October 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Dexter |first1=Giles |title=Te Pāti Māori to suspend MP Mariameno Kapa-Kingi – reports |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/577010/te-pati-maori-to-suspend-mp-mariameno-kapa-kingi-reports |access-date=28 October 2025 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=27 October 2025}}</ref>

Between late October and early November 2025, former executive member Amokura Panoho and former vice-president Eru Kapa-Kingi called for John Tamihere's resignation as party president.<ref>{{cite news |title=Founding member of Te Pāti Māori calls for Tamihere's resignation|url=https://newsroom.co.nz/2025/10/31/founding-member-of-te-pati-maori-calls-for-john-tamiheres-resignation/ |access-date=1 November 2025 |work=[[Newsroom (website)|Newsroom]] |date=31 October 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251110222646/https://newsroom.co.nz/2025/10/31/founding-member-of-te-pati-maori-calls-for-john-tamiheres-resignation/|archive-date=10 November 2025|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Hanly |first1=Lilian |title=Former Te Pāti Māori staffer Eru Kapa-Kingi doubles down on leadership shortcomings |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/578192/former-te-pati-maori-staffer-eru-kapa-kingi-doubles-down-on-leadership-shortcomings |access-date=11 November 2025 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=9 November 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251109221056/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/578192/former-te-pati-maori-staffer-eru-kapa-kingi-doubles-down-on-leadership-shortcomings |archive-date=9 November 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> On 3 November, Tamihere publicly called on Mariameno Kapa-Kingi and [[Tākuta Ferris]], MP for [[Te Tai Tonga]], to resign, claiming that in July 2025 the pair had conspired to oust and replace party leaders Ngarewa-Packer and Waititi.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Dexter |first=Giles |date=3 November 2025 |title='Greed, avarice, and entitlement' – Te Pāti Māori president urges MPs to quit |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-manu-korihi/577653/greed-avarice-and-entitlement-te-pati-maori-president-urges-mps-to-quit |access-date=9 November 2025 |work=[[RNZ]] |language=en-nz |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251109221244/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-manu-korihi/577653/greed-avarice-and-entitlement-te-pati-maori-president-urges-mps-to-quit|archive-date=9 November 2025|url-status=live}}</ref> Amidst tensions between the party leadership and Kapa-Kingi and Ferris, the [[National Iwi Chairs Forum]] met with Waititi and Ngarewa-Packer on 4 November in an attempt to defuse tensions within the party.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Cugley |first1=Michael |title=Iwi Chairs intervene as Te Pāti Māori faces internal divisions |url=https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2025/11/05/iwi-chairs-intervene-as-te-pati-maori-faces-internal-divisions/ |access-date=11 November 2025 |work=[[Te Ao Māori News]] |date=5 November 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251111000733/https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2025/11/05/iwi-chairs-intervene-as-te-pati-maori-faces-internal-divisions/ |archive-date=11 November 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>

On 9 November, the national council of Te Pāti Māori voted to expel both Mariameno Kapa-Kingi and Ferris.<ref name=":9">{{cite news|url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/578378/te-pati-maori-expels-takuta-ferris-and-mariameno-kapa-kingi|title=Te Pāti Māori expels Tākuta Ferris and Mariameno Kapa-Kingi|publisher=[[RNZ]]|date=10 November 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251110042905/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-manu-korihi/578378/te-pati-maori-expels-takuta-ferris-and-mariameno-kapa-kingi|archive-date=10 November 2025|url-status=live}}</ref> Ferris called the decision "plainly unconstitutional" and Kapa-Kingi said she would appeal.<ref name=":9" /> On 11 November, former party co-leader [[Te Ururoa Flavell]] questioned the voting process behind the expulsion of the two MPs, citing the exclusion of representatives from Kapa-Kingi's Te Tai Tokerau electorate and the abstention of representatives from the [[Hauraki-Waikato]] electorate and Ferris's Te Tai Tonga electorate.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Dexter |first1=Giles |last2=Hanly |first2=Lilian |title=Te Pāti Māori MPs' expulsions questioned by law expert, former co-leader |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/578450/te-pati-maori-mps-expulsions-questioned-by-law-expert-former-co-leader |access-date=10 November 2025 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=11 November 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251110235834/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/578450/te-pati-maori-mps-expulsions-questioned-by-law-expert-former-co-leader |archive-date=10 November 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> On 19 November, former Māori Party MP [[Hone Harawira]] called for Kapa-Kingi and Ferris to be reinstated as members and for a national reconciliation tour.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hanly |first1=Lillian |title=Former MP Hone Harawira weighs in on Te Pāti Māori turmoil |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-manu-korihi/579326/former-mp-hone-harawira-weighs-in-on-te-pati-maori-turmoil |access-date=20 November 2025 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=19 November 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251120010120/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-manu-korihi/579326/former-mp-hone-harawira-weighs-in-on-te-pati-maori-turmoil |archive-date=20 November 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>

On 4 December 2025, Kapa-Kingi filed an interim injunction at the [[High Court of New Zealand|Wellington High Court]] challenging Te Pāti Māori's decision to expel her.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Day |first1=Tom |title=Mariameno Kapa-Kingi challenges Te Pati Maori expulsion |url=https://www.1news.co.nz/2025/12/04/mariameno-kapa-kingi-challenges-te-pati-maori-expulsion/ |access-date=5 December 2025 |work=[[1News]] |date=4 December 2025}}</ref> Her legal team argued that her suspension and expulsion process violated the party's constitution and basic principles of fairness. Key arguments included that no proper disciplinary body had been constituted, that no adequate hearing or notice was provided, and that her membership cancellation process was unfair.<ref name="Waatea News 5 Dec 2025">{{cite news |title=Kapa‑Kingi v Tamihere – Kapa‑Kingi returned |url=https://waateanews.com/2025/12/05/kapa%e2%80%91kingi-v-tamihere-kapa%e2%80%91kingi-returned/ |access-date=6 December 2025 |work=[[Radio Waatea|Waatea News]] |date=5 December 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251206035227/https://waateanews.com/2025/12/05/kapa%E2%80%91kingi-v-tamihere-kapa%E2%80%91kingi-returned/|archive-date=6 December 2025|url-status=live}}</ref> The following day, Justice Paul Radich  reinstated Kapa-Kingi's membership of the party. However, Radich declined her three other requests, which included removing Tamihere as Te Pāti Māori's president, stopping the party's annual general meeting scheduled for 6–7 December, and preventing the party's national council and executive from passing further resolutions.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hanly |first1=Lillian |title=Mariameno Kapa-Kingi reinstated as a member of Te Pāti Māori in interim High Court ruling |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-manu-korihi/581016/mariameno-kapa-kingi-reinstated-as-a-member-of-te-pati-maori-in-interim-high-court-ruling |access-date=6 December 2025 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=5 December 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251205094726/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-manu-korihi/581016/mariameno-kapa-kingi-reinstated-as-a-member-of-te-pati-maori-in-interim-high-court-ruling |archive-date=5 December 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Te Pāti Māori's 2025 annual general meeting was held on 7 December at [[Waiatuhi]] marae in [[Rotorua]], which was attended by 200 people including Kapa-Kingi. During the AGM, president Tamihere identified the National-led coalition government as the party's enemy. Several speakers including former [[Māori King movement|Kiingitanga]] spokesperson Ngira Simmonds raised the issue of disunity and infighting within the party, with Simmonds questioning Tamihere, Waititi and Ngarewa-Packer's suitability to lead Te Pāti Māori.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hanly |first1=Lillian |title=Ngira Simmonds challenges Te Pāti Māori leadership at AGM |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/top/581120/ngira-simmonds-challenges-te-pati-maori-leadership-at-agm |access-date=9 December 2025 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=7 December 2025}}</ref>

During [[Waitangi Day]] on 5 February 2026, Kapa-Kingi used his korero (speech) to question the presence of political parties and the [[New Zealand Crown]] on the [[Waitangi, Northland|Waitangi]] Treaty grounds, and urged Te Pāti Māori to "sort yourselves out".<ref>{{cite news |title=Tensions flare at Waitangi as haka confronts Eru Kapa-Kingi |url= https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2026/02/05/tensions-flare-at-waitangi-as-haka-confronts-eru-kapa-kingi/ |access-date=23 March 2026 |work=[[Te Ao Māori News]] |date=5 February 2026}}</ref> In response, Waititi delivered an address, which Kapa-Kingi regarded as a "half-pai apology." Waititi's wife Kiri Tamihere-Waititi and other Te Pāti Māori sympathizers then delivered a retaliatory [[haka]] in challenge. Tamihere-Waiti strode across the marae during said haka and came very close to Kapa-Kingi, which he regarded as a spiritual attack on himself and his family. Kapa-Kingi said the confrontation destroyed all hope of reconciliation with Te Pāti Māori and that he could no longer support them.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Marriner |first1=Chris |title='Pokokohua koe': Eru Kapa-Kingi curses Te Pāti Māori, vows to never support them after challenge|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/nz-news/360946365/pokokohua-koe-eru-kapa-kingi-curses-te-pati-maori-vows-never-support-them-after-waitangi-challenge|work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=4 March 2026}}</ref>

On 10 March 2026, Te Pāti Māori stated it would comply with Justice Radich's order to reinstate Kapa-Kingi's party membership, allowing her to participate in party meetings and functions.<ref>{{cite news |last1=McConnell |first1=Glenn |title=Court orders that Mariameno Kapa-Kingi be reinstated to Te Pāti Māori |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360949198/court-orders-mariameno-kapa-kingi-be-reinstated-te-pati-maori |access-date=10 March 2026 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=10 March 2026}}</ref> Despite her court-mandated reinstatement, [[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] reported on 8 May that Kapa-Kingi and Te Pāti Māori were still not working and that she still shared an office space with fellow former TPM MP Ferris. Both of the party's electorate committee in Kapa-Kingi and Ferris's electorates – Te Tai Tokerau and Te Tai Tonga – also resigned and expressed support for Kapa-Kingi and Ferris; depriving the party of the infrastructure needed to select new candidates in those electorates.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=McConnell |first1=Glenn |title=Te Pāti Māori in crisis, MPs could walk out ahead of election| url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360976177/te-pati-maori-crisis-mps-could-walk-out-ahead-election |access-date=11 May 2026 |date=8 May 2026 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]]}}</ref>

On 11 May 2026, Kapa-Kingi announced that she would start her own party called the [[Te Tai Tokerau Party]] to contest the [[2026 New Zealand general election]]. The party acknowledged her departure and reiterated its commitment to contesting all seven Māori electorates during the 2026 general election.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Rebel MP Mariameno Kapa-Kingi quitting Te Pāti Māori to start own party | url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360977114/former-te-pati-maori-mp-kapa-kingi-start-own-political-party |access-date=11 May 2026 |date=11 May 2026 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Dunlop |first1=Māni |title=Mariameno Kapa-Kingi leaves Te Pāti Māori, launches new political party |url=https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2026/05/11/mariameno-kapa-kingi-leaves-te-pati-maori-announces-new-political-party/ |access-date=12 May 2026 |work=[[Te Ao Māori News]] |date=11 May 2026 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20260512000532/https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2026/05/11/mariameno-kapa-kingi-leaves-te-pati-maori-announces-new-political-party/ |archive-date=12 May 2026|url-status=live}}</ref>

==== 2026 general election ====
In January 2026, Te Pāti Māori said that they will campaign on [[prison abolition|abolishing prisons]] by 2040 to address the high Māori incarceration rate, replacing them with so-called "community-led and community-based solutions".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gabel |first1=Julia |title=Election 2026: Te Pāti Māori to campaign on abolishing prisons, Labour dead-set against it |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/election-2026-te-pati-maori-to-campaign-on-abolishing-prisons-labour-dead-set-against-it/25RU6JTA7JDVVDHLV6AS7ONMNQ/ |access-date=26 January 2026 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=26 January 2026}}</ref> On 27 May, Te Pāti Māori announced  Ngātiwai Trust Board chairman Aperahama Edwards as its candidate for [[Te Tai Tokerau]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Crimp |first1=Lauren |title=Aperahama Edwards to run for Te Pāti Māori in Te Tai Tokerau |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/596458/aperahama-edwards-to-run-for-te-pati-maori-in-te-tai-tokerau |access-date=26 July 2026 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=27 May 2026}}</ref> In late June 2026, the party's leadership confirmed that they would encourage Māori voters to register for the [[Māori electorates|Māori roll]] and urged their supporters to give their electorate vote to Te Pāti Māori and their party vote to either Labour or the Greens.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Natanahira |first1=Tuwhenuaroa |title=Te Pāti Māori lay out their strategy to defeat the coalition |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/617536/te-pati-maori-lay-out-their-strategy-to-defeat-the-coalition |access-date=26 July 2026 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=23 July 2026}}</ref> 

Te Pāti Māori launched its electoral campaign on 16 August.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Natanahira |first1=Tuwhenuaroa |title=Te Pāti Māori reveals election strategy as campaign launches in Gisborne |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1011909/te-pati-maori-reveals-election-strategy-as-campaign-launches-in-gisborne |access-date=17 August 2026 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=16 August 2026}}</ref> In late August 2026, the party announced its tax policies which included a 48% tax rate on those earning NZ$300,001 and above, a rebate for New Zealanders earning less than NZ$30,000, various wealth, company, land banking and vacant home taxes, and a stamp duty.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ricketts |first1=Emma |title=Te Pāti Māori proposes 48% income tax rate, tax credit for kai |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/361025236/te-pati-maori-proposes-48-income-tax-rate-tax-credit-kai |access-date=30 August 2026 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=26 August 2026}}</ref> On 1 September, the party released several constitutional reform policies including establishing an independent "Te Tiriti Commission" to investigate alleged breaches of the [[Treaty of Waitangi]] by the [[New Zealand Crown]], making [[Waitangi Tribunal]] recommendations legally binding, establishing a 2040 target for constitutional reform and establishing a $200 million Matike Mai Fund to implement these reforms and the [[United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples]] (UNDRIP).<ref>{{cite news |last1=Natanahira |first1=Tuwhenuaroa |title=Te Pāti Māori vows major constitutional reform by making Te Tiriti binding for Crown|url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1207353/te-pati-maori-vows-major-constitutional-reform-by-making-te-tiriti-binding-for-crown|access-date=7 September 2026 |work=[[RNZ]] |date=1 September 2026}}</ref> While Labour has ruled out supporting a Te Tiriti Commission and Mātike Mai, the Greens said that Te Pāti Māori's proposed constitutional reforms aligned with its own Treaty of Waitangi policies. NZ First and ACT have denounced these constitutional reform policies as divisive and wasteful.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Dunlop |first1=Mani |title=Te Pāti Māori’s Te Tiriti entrenchment plan: How would it work, and could it happen? |url=https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2026/09/02/te-pati-maoris-te-tiriti-entrenchment-plan-how-would-it-work-and-could-it-happen/ |access-date=9 September 2026 |work=[[Te Ao Māori News]] |date=2 September 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260906194000/https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2026/09/02/te-pati-maoris-te-tiriti-entrenchment-plan-how-would-it-work-and-could-it-happen/|archive-date=6 September 2026|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Principles and policy ==

The party is committed to advancing what it sees as the [[minority rights|rights]] and interests of the Māori, the indigenous people of New Zealand. Increasingly since the beginning of colonisation, Māori have been marginalised and the group is now a minority within New Zealand alongside Pacific Islanders.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pearson |first=David |date=5 May 2011 |title=Ethnic Inequalities in New Zealand |url=https://teara.govt.nz/en/ethnic-inequalities/page-2 |access-date=9 May 2018 |website=Te Ara |archive-date=11 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230811020654/https://teara.govt.nz/en/ethnic-inequalities/page-2 |url-status=live }}</ref> Te Pāti Māori policy focuses particularly on [[New Zealand property bubble|affordable housing]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Māori Party Housing Policy 2017 |url=http://www.maoriparty.org/housing_policy_2017 |access-date=9 May 2018 |website=Māori Party |archive-date=10 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180510115800/http://www.maoriparty.org/housing_policy_2017 |url-status=live }}</ref> Māori recruitment into [[tertiary education in New Zealand|tertiary institutes]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Māori Party Education Policy 2017 |url=http://www.maoriparty.org/education_policy_2017 |access-date=9 May 2018 |website=Māori Party |archive-date=9 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180809042029/http://www.maoriparty.org/education_policy_2017 |url-status=live }}</ref> and a [[living wage]] for all workers,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Māori Party Employment Policy 2017 |url=http://www.maoriparty.org/employment_policy_2017 |access-date=9 May 2018 |website=Māori Party |archive-date=10 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180510115855/http://www.maoriparty.org/employment_policy_2017 |url-status=live }}</ref> based on the premise that Māori are among the low-socioeconomic communities in New Zealand who are the most economically disadvantaged.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pollock |first=Kerryn |date=5 May 2011 |title=Health and Society in New Zealand: Socio-economic status, ethnicity and health inequality |url=https://teara.govt.nz/en/health-and-society/page-2 |access-date=9 May 2018 |website=Te Ara |archive-date=11 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230811011655/https://teara.govt.nz/en/health-and-society/page-2 |url-status=live }}</ref> During the 2020s, Te Pāti Māori has been widely described as [[Progressivism|progressive]],<ref name="auto" /><ref name=":6" /><ref name=":5" /> and further to the political left than [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour]] by [[Al Jazeera English|Al Jazeera]]<ref name="auto1" /> and [[Newshub]].<ref name=":5" /> Previously, during its years in alliance with [[New Zealand National Party|National]], the party had been described as [[centrist]].<ref>{{cite book |editor=Morgan Godfery |title=Māui Street |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tbd6DwAAQBAJ&dq=centrist+M%C4%81ori+Party&pg=PA43 |quote=... of the centrist Māori Party, told media that her party 'cannot support [Clark's] nomination [for Secretary-General]'. ... |date=2018 |page=43 |publisher=[[Bridget Williams Books]] |isbn=978-1-988545-45-5}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Dann |first1=Liam |title=Disenchanted Right finds a voice at last |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/business/liam-dann-disenchanted-right-finds-a-voice-at-last/QD4XKZRSHSVIJTDQVR26GFEBBY/ |access-date=12 February 2023 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=29 April 2011 |language=en-NZ |quote=...a pretty sensible and centrist Maori party. |archive-date=11 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230211174439/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/business/liam-dann-disenchanted-right-finds-a-voice-at-last/QD4XKZRSHSVIJTDQVR26GFEBBY/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

The Māori Party was formed in response to the [[New Zealand foreshore and seabed controversy|2004 foreshore and seabed controversy]], a debate about whether Māori have legitimate claim to ownership of part or all of New Zealand's foreshore and seabed. The founders of the party believed that:

* Māori owned the foreshore and seabed before British colonisation;
* {{lang|mi|[[Te Tiriti o Waitangi]] | italics=no}} made no specific mention of foreshore or seabed;
* No-one has subsequently purchased or otherwise acquired the foreshore or the seabed; and
* Māori should therefore still own the seabed and the foreshore today.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hickford |first1=Mark |title=Law of the foreshore and seabed – Māori rights |url=https://www.teara.govt.nz/en/law-of-the-foreshore-and-seabed/page-2 |publisher=e Ara – the Encyclopedia of New Zealand |access-date=8 October 2017 |archive-date=11 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230811052924/https://teara.govt.nz/en/law-of-the-foreshore-and-seabed/page-2 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Hickford |first1=Mark |title=Law of the foreshore and seabed – Challenge and controversy |url=https://www.teara.govt.nz/en/law-of-the-foreshore-and-seabed/page-4 |publisher=Te Ara – the Encyclopedia of New Zealand |access-date=8 October 2017 |archive-date=10 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230810233924/https://teara.govt.nz/en/law-of-the-foreshore-and-seabed/page-4 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The {{lang|mi|kaupapa}} (policy platform) of Te Pāti Māori is based on four principles or pillars:<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.maoriparty.org/our_kaupapa |title=Māori Party Kaupapa |website=Māori Party |access-date=9 May 2018 |archive-date=10 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180510115423/http://www.maoriparty.org/our_kaupapa |url-status=live }}</ref>
* {{lang|mi|[[Whānau]] | italics=no}} (includes policies regarding affordable housing,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.maoriparty.org/housing_policy_2017 |title=Māori Party Housing Policy 2017 |access-date=9 May 2018 |archive-date=10 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180510115800/http://www.maoriparty.org/housing_policy_2017 |url-status=live }}</ref> strengthening employment-support for Māori beneficiaries<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.maoriparty.org/employment_policy_2017 |title=Māori Party Employment Policy 2017 |access-date=9 May 2018 |archive-date=10 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180510115855/http://www.maoriparty.org/employment_policy_2017 |url-status=live }}</ref> and [[te reo Māori]])<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.maoriparty.org/te_reo_maori_policy_2017 |title=Māori Party Te Reo Māori Policy 2017 |access-date=9 May 2018 |archive-date=10 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180510183900/http://www.maoriparty.org/te_reo_maori_policy_2017 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* [[Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi|Te Tiriti o Waitangi principles]] (includes holding [[the Crown]] accountable to their obligations under {{lang|mi|Te Tiriti o Waitangi|italics=no}}, and policies on immigration)<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.maoriparty.org/immigration_policy_2017 |title=Māori Party Immigration Policy 2017 |access-date=9 May 2018 |archive-date=10 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180510184024/http://www.maoriparty.org/immigration_policy_2017 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* {{lang|mi|[[Rangatiratanga]] | italics=no}} (includes policies on climate change in the Pacific and scholarships for Māori and Pasifika education to advance Māori and Pasifika as a collective)<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.maoriparty.org/pasefika_policy_2017 |title=Māori Party Pasefika Policy 2017 |access-date=9 May 2018 |archive-date=10 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180510183927/http://www.maoriparty.org/pasefika_policy_2017 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* {{lang|mi|[[Kāwanatanga]] | italics=no}} (includes policies on growing [[iwi]] economic resources<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.maoriparty.org/economic_policy_2017 |title=Māori Party Economic Policy 2017 |access-date=9 May 2018 |archive-date=10 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180510184217/http://www.maoriparty.org/economic_policy_2017 |url-status=live }}</ref> and to protect freshwater as a {{lang|mi|[[taonga]]}})<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.maoriparty.org/environment_policy_2017 |title=Māori Party Environment Policy |access-date=9 May 2018 |archive-date=10 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180510115614/http://www.maoriparty.org/environment_policy_2017 |url-status=live }}</ref>

These principles enable Te Pāti Māori to be held accountable for the maintenance and furthering of Māori concepts in the decision-making process. These concepts are not reflected in the traditional [[Westminster system]] and Māori [[customary law]] is excluded from the New Zealand general legal system.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jackson |first=Moana |year=1990 |title=Criminality and the Exclusion of Māori |journal=Victoria University of Wellington Law Review |volume=20 |pages=27–29}}</ref> Other Māori-rights-specific party policies have included the upholding of "indigenous values"<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.maoriparty.org/index.php?pag=cms&id=130&p=election-policy.html |title=Election Policy 2008 |publisher=Māori Party |access-date=5 October 2011 |quote=Our commitment to you is that we will uphold indigenous values, to ensure our country maintains its natural beauty for all who call this land home. |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130216215837/http://www.maoriparty.org/index.php?pag=cms&id=130&p=election-policy.html |archive-date=16 February 2013 }}</ref> and compulsory "heritage studies" in schools.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.maoriparty.org/index.php?pag=cms&id=130&p=election-policy.html |title=Election Policy 2008 |publisher=Māori Party |access-date=5 October 2011 |quote=Primary and secondary schools will be required to teach heritage studies, which will include a history of the Pacific, in line with the aspirations of Pacific people. |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130216215837/http://www.maoriparty.org/index.php?pag=cms&id=130&p=election-policy.html |archive-date=16 February 2013 }}</ref>

Since 2022 the party has advocated for the abolition of the British monarchy, when the party called for [[Queen Elizabeth II]] to be removed as [[monarchy of New Zealand|New Zealand's head of state]] on [[Waitangi Day]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/taranaki-daily-news/news/300511893/te-pti-mori-seek-divorce-from-britains-monarchy |title=Te Pāti Māori seek "divorce" from Britain's monarchy |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=6 February 2022 |access-date=7 February 2022 |archive-date=10 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230810230339/https://www.stuff.co.nz/taranaki-daily-news/news/300511893/te-pti-mori-seek-divorce-from-britains-monarchy |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/waitangi-day-te-pati-maori-calls-for-divorce-from-british-monarchy/N5H3WQRHHIKBIDZDOLHA6ZKAJQ/ |title=Waitangi Day: Te Pāti Māori calls for "divorce" from British monarchy |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=5 February 2022 |access-date=7 February 2022 |archive-date=10 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230810233843/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/waitangi-day-te-pati-maori-calls-for-divorce-from-british-monarchy/N5H3WQRHHIKBIDZDOLHA6ZKAJQ/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The party advocates for the establishment of a  Māori parliament.<ref name="devolution" /> The party has several policies to ensure Māori ownership of land, including transferring all Crown land to iwi, ending all perpetual leases and establishing a [[right of first refusal]] for iwi on all private land.<ref>{{cite web |title=Mana Motuhake Policy |url=https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y9GTi2VGAYIJygAmaQ5e-WVCLYlCOYTL/view |website=Te Pāti Māori Mana Motuhake Policy |publisher=Te Pāti Māori |access-date=11 August 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Treaty claim reset in Maori Party plan |url=https://waateanews.com/2020/09/29/treaty-claim-reset-in-maori-party-plan/ |work=Waatea team |publisher=Waatea News |date=29 September 202}}</ref>

The party is committed to a mixture of socially progressive and [[Environmentalism|environmentalist]] policy through a "[[Treaty of Waitangi|Titiri-centric]]" Māori lens.<ref name=":3" />  The party is committed to removing [[Goods and Services Tax (New Zealand)|Goods and Services Tax]] from food, opposing [[Deep Sea Drilling Project|deep sea drilling]], organising and funding a [[Māori Health Authority|Māori health authority]] and reducing [[Homelessness in New Zealand|homelessness]] in Māori communities.<ref name=":4" /> During the [[2026 New Zealand general election|2026 general election]], the party campaigned on [[prison abolition|abolishing prisons]] by 2040 in favour of community-led solutions to address the high Māori incarceration rate.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gabel |first1=Julia |title=Election 2026: Te Pāti Māori to campaign on abolishing prisons, Labour dead-set against it |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/election-2026-te-pati-maori-to-campaign-on-abolishing-prisons-labour-dead-set-against-it/25RU6JTA7JDVVDHLV6AS7ONMNQ/ |access-date=26 January 2026 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=26 January 2026}}</ref>

=== Renaming New Zealand ===

In September 2021 the party launched an online petition to change the country's official name to "[[Aotearoa]]", and to officially restore Māori-language names for all [[List of New Zealand place name etymologies|place names]].<ref name="Change official name">{{cite web |title=Change our official name to Aotearoa |url=https://www.maoriparty.org.nz/nz_to_aotearoa |publisher=Māori Party |access-date=19 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210917163819/https://www.maoriparty.org.nz/nz_to_aotearoa |archive-date=17 September 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Guy |first=Jack |title=Māori Party campaigns to change New Zealand's name to Aotearoa |url=https://edition.cnn.com/travel/article/new-zealand-aotearoa-name-change-scli-intl/index.html |access-date=19 September 2021 |work=[[CNN]] |date=15 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210918042142/https://edition.cnn.com/travel/article/new-zealand-aotearoa-name-change-scli-intl/index.html |archive-date=18 September 2021}}</ref> In its statement is mentioned Article 3 of the Treaty of Waitangi which gave the Māori language equal status with English.<ref name="Change official name" /> By early June 2022, the petition had over 70,000 signatures, and was to be submitted to Parliament's petitions committee. Waititi argued that the change would recognise New Zealand's indigenous heritage and strengthen its identity as a Pacific country. He opposed the idea of a referendum, claiming it would entrench the "tyranny of the majority".<ref>{{cite news |last=McConnell |first=Glenn |title=Māori Party petition to officially call the country Aotearoa gets 70,000 supporters |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/128845298/mori-party-petition-to-officially-call-the-country-aotearoa-gets-70000-supporters |access-date=3 June 2022 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=2 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220604110100/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/128845298/mori-party-petition-to-officially-call-the-country-aotearoa-gets-70000-supporters |archive-date=4 June 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Foreign policy issues ===

In May 2021, Te Pāti Māori co-leaders Ngarewa-Packer and Waititi supported Green member of parliament [[Golriz Ghahraman]]'s push for New Zealand to recognise the [[State of Palestine]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Small |first1=Zane |title=Te Pāti Māori co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer shuts down heckler at pro-Palestine march |url=https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2021/05/te-p-ti-m-ori-co-leader-debbie-ngarewa-packer-shuts-down-heckler-at-pro-palestine-march.html |access-date=31 October 2023 |work=[[Newshub]] |date=19 May 2021 |archive-date=31 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231031015231/https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2021/05/te-p-ti-m-ori-co-leader-debbie-ngarewa-packer-shuts-down-heckler-at-pro-palestine-march.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> During the [[Gaza war]], Te Pāti Māori advocated expulsion of the Israeli ambassador if Israel did not implement a ceasefire or open a humanitarian corridor in Gaza.<ref>{{cite web |author1=Te Pāti Māori |title=Te Pāti Māori Demand NZ Government Expel Israeli Ambassador If There Is No Immediate Ceasefire, Humanitarian Aid |url=https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2310/S00089/te-pati-maori-demand-nz-government-expel-israeli-ambassador-if-there-is-no-immediate-ceasefire-humanitarian-aid.htm |publisher=[[Scoop (website)|Scoop]] |access-date=31 October 2023 |date=18 October 2023 |archive-date=24 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231124145348/https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2310/S00089/te-pati-maori-demand-nz-government-expel-israeli-ambassador-if-there-is-no-immediate-ceasefire-humanitarian-aid.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> Ngarewa-Packer also defended Green MP [[Chlöe Swarbrick]]'s controversial "[[From the river to the sea]]" statement and urged the caretaker Labour Government to call for an "end to war crimes."<ref>{{cite news |last1=McConnell |first1=Glenn |title='A very loaded statement': Chris Hipkins expects Labour MPs to avoid 'river to sea' chant |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/133250410/a-very-loaded-statement-chris-hipkins-expects-labour-mps-to-avoid-river-to-sea-chant |access-date=26 January 2024 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=7 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231124030643/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/133250410/a-very-loaded-statement-chris-hipkins-expects-labour-mps-to-avoid-river-to-sea-chant |archive-date=24 November 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Leadership ==
{{Main|Co-leaders of Te Pāti Māori}}
{{As of|2020|}}, the constitution of Te Pāti Māori states that it must have two leaders, that its co-leaders must be drawn from its MPs first, and that one must be female and one male.<ref name=":0" /> These requirements have been in place since at least 2013.<ref name=":1" />

The party's first leaders were Tariana Turia and Pita Sharples. In December 2012, Turia announced she would resign as party co-leader before the 2014 general election. Te Ururoa Flavell announced his interest in a leadership role, but as the Māori Party constitution required male and female co-leaders, he could not take Turia's place.<ref name=":1">"[http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/8171818/Ratana-unveiling-for-Turias-successor Ratana unveiling for Turia's successor?] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130116171828/http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/8171818/Ratana-unveiling-for-Turias-successor |date=16 January 2013 }}". ''[[The Dominion Post (New Zealand)|The Dominion Post]]''. 13 January 2013</ref> Shortly after this, in July 2013, Sharples resigned as co-leader, saying he would quit politics altogether come the next general election in 2014. He went on to say that "Our supporters deserve a unified party" which indicated that the leadership tension influenced his decision to resign as party co-leader.<ref>{{cite news |title=Pita Sharples stands down, Flavell likely successor |url=http://tvnz.co.nz/politics-news/pita-sharples-stands-down-flavell-likely-successor-5483970 |work=One News |date=2 July 2013 |access-date=31 August 2014 |archive-date=29 November 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129133011/http://tvnz.co.nz/politics-news/pita-sharples-stands-down-flavell-likely-successor-5483970 |url-status=live }}</ref> Flavell replaced him as the party's male co-leader. In the [[2014 New Zealand general election|2014 general election]], Marama Fox became the party's first [[list MP]], and – as the party's only female MP – under the party rules automatically became female co-leader.

Following Rawiri Waititi's successful campaign for [[Waiariki (New Zealand electorate)|Waiariki]] at the [[2020 New Zealand general election]], he was confirmed as male co-leader, replacing John Tamihere, at a special general meeting of the Māori Party on 28 October.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/429357/maori-party-s-rawiri-waititi-replaces-john-tamihere-as-co-leader |title=Māori Party's Rawiri Waititi replaces John Tamihere as co-leader |work=[[RNZ News]] |date=29 October 2020 |access-date=8 November 2020 |archive-date=1 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201101083903/https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/429357/maori-party-s-rawiri-waititi-replaces-john-tamihere-as-co-leader |url-status=live }}</ref>
